questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the inferior boundary (floor) of Hesselbach's (inguinal) triangle?
options: Medial half of the inguinal ligament
questions.explanation: Hesselbach's triangle is bounded medially by the rectus abdominis, superolaterally by the inferior epigastric artery, and inferiorly by the medial half of the inguinal ligament.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structure forms the upper boundary (roof) of the omental foramen (foramen of Winslow)?
options: Caudate process of the caudate lobe of the liver
Right free margin of the lesser omentum
questions.explanation: The caudate process of the caudate lobe forms the superior boundary of the epiploic (omental) foramen.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structure suspends the duodenojejunal flexure from the right crus of the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: The duodenojejunal flexure is anchored to the right crus of the diaphragm by the suspensory muscle.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which surface of the spleen bears the gastric, renal, colic, and pancreatic impressions?
questions.explanation: The medial visceral surface of the spleen features impressions for the stomach, left kidney, left colic flexure, and tail of the pancreas.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, which vagal nerves provide parasympathetic supply to the stomach?
options: Anterior and posterior gastric nerves, from the left and right vagus respectively
questions.explanation: The anterior and posterior gastric nerves are identified as vagal branches from the left and right vagus, respectively.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: At the porta hepatis, which structure is positioned posteriorly in the lecture's arrangement?
options: Right and left portal vein branches
Right and left hepatic artery branches
questions.explanation: The portal vein branches are posterior; the hepatic ducts are anterior and hepatic artery branches are in the middle.

questions.stem: What is the primary sensory modality to which the rectum and upper anal canal respond?

questions.stem: What is the shape of the root of the sigmoid mesocolon attached to the posterior pelvic wall?

questions.stem: Where does lymphatic drainage from the lower half of the anal canal primarily go?

questions.stem: Where does venous blood from the superior rectal vein ultimately drain?

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the upper third of the rectum?

questions.stem: Which part of the levator ani muscle forms a sling around the anorectal junction to create the anorectal angle?
questions.explanation: The puborectalis part of the levator ani forms a U-shaped sling that pulls the anorectal junction forward, creating an acute anorectal angle.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which peritoneal pouch is formed behind the urinary bladder in the female?
questions.explanation: In females, the peritoneum reflects from the bladder to the uterus, forming the uterovesical pouch.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which vessels provide arterial blood to the upper parts of the urinary bladder?
options: Superior vesical artery (from the umbilical artery)
questions.explanation: The superior vesical artery branches from the obliterated umbilical artery to supply the bladder.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is the mucosal surface of the trigone of the bladder characteristically smooth?
options: Because it is lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium
Because it lacks a muscular coat entirely
Because it is composed of elastic tissue and firmly attached to the muscular coat
Because it is covered by a thick layer of peritoneum
questions.explanation: The trigone remains smooth because it is composed of elastic tissue firmly anchored to the underlying muscle, preventing the formation of rugae.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In which direction does the anal canal pass from the anorectal junction toward the anus?
questions.explanation: The anal canal passes downward and backward from the anorectal junction.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: The inferior rectal vein drains first into which vein, as described in the slides?
questions.explanation: The inferior rectal vein drains into the internal pudendal vein before reaching the internal iliac vein and systemic circulation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What configuration do the puborectalis fibres form around the anorectal junction?
options: A complete circular ring around the anal verge
A straight band between the ischial tuberosities
A V-shaped ligament behind the coccyx
questions.explanation: The puborectalis fibres blend with the deep external sphincter to form a U-shaped sling.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What forms the anterior boundary of the ischiorectal fossa?
options: Superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles
questions.explanation: The anterior boundary is formed by the superficial and deep transverse perineal muscles.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What forms the pudendal canal?
options: A splitting of the obturator fascia
A tunnel through the sacrotuberous ligament
A passage through the levator ani
A division of the perineal membrane
questions.explanation: The pudendal canal is a tunnel formed by splitting of the obturator fascia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the posterior relation of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The slide identifies the anococcygeal body as the posterior relation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Where does the outer longitudinal smooth-muscle layer of the anal canal descend?
options: Between the internal and external anal sphincters
Between the two layers of the bladder wall
questions.explanation: The outer longitudinal layer continues from the rectum and descends in the interval between the two anal sphincters.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which artery supplies the lower half of the anal canal according to the slides?
questions.explanation: The lower half is supplied by the inferior rectal artery, a branch of the internal pudendal artery.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which epithelial lining characterizes the lower half of the anal canal in the lecture slides?
questions.explanation: The lower half is lined by stratified squamous epithelium and lacks anal columns and valves.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which lymph nodes receive lymph from the upper half of the anal canal in the slide table?
options: Superior rectal nodes, then pararectal and inferior mesenteric nodes
Deep inguinal nodes, then external iliac nodes
questions.explanation: The upper-half pathway runs through superior rectal nodes and pararectal nodes to inferior mesenteric nodes.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which named nerve and vessels are contents of the ischiorectal fossa?
questions.explanation: The fossa contains the inferior rectal nerve and vessels; the pudendal nerve and internal pudendal vessels lie within the pudendal canal.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which nerve supply is specified for the external anal sphincter?
options: Inferior rectal nerve and perineal branch of S4
questions.explanation: The external sphincter receives the inferior rectal nerve (from the pudendal nerve) and the perineal branch of S4.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structure is listed as an anterior relation of the anal canal?
questions.explanation: The perineal body and urogenital diaphragm are the stated anterior relations of the anal canal.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structures are contained in the anal triangle of the perineum?
options: The anal canal and ischiorectal fossae
The urethra and external genitalia only
questions.explanation: The anal triangle contains the anal canal and the ischiorectal fossae.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which structures form the lateral wall of the ischiorectal fossa?
options: Obturator internus, obturator fascia, and pudendal canal
questions.explanation: The lateral wall is formed by obturator internus, its fascia, and the pudendal canal.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which territory is supplied by the perineal nerve, a branch of the pudendal nerve?
options: Urogenital triangle muscles and skin on the posterior scrotum or labia majora
Lower half of the anal canal and perianal skin only
Levator ani and skin over the sacrum
questions.explanation: The perineal nerve supplies muscles of the urogenital triangle and skin on the posterior scrotum or labia majora.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A brachial plexus with a major contribution from C4 is described in the lecture as which variant?
questions.explanation: The lecture calls the plexus prefixed when it has a major C4 contribution; a major T2 contribution is termed postfixed.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: After crossing the anatomical snuffbox, through which interval does the radial artery enter the palm?
options: Between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous
Between the two heads of pronator teres
Between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
questions.explanation: The radial artery enters the palm between the two heads of the first dorsal interosseous muscle.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: At the wrist, how does the ulnar nerve enter the hand relative to the flexor retinaculum?
options: Deep to it through the carpal tunnel
Superficial to it, just lateral to the pisiform
Between the two heads of pronator teres
questions.explanation: The ulnar nerve passes over the flexor retinaculum, just lateral to the pisiform, before dividing in the hand.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: At which landmark does the nutrient artery of the humerus enter the bone?
questions.explanation: The lecture places the humeral nutrient artery entry at the insertion of coracobrachialis.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does the median nerve enter the forearm from the cubital fossa?
options: Between the two heads of pronator teres
Behind the medial epicondyle between the heads of flexor carpi ulnaris
Between the heads of the first dorsal interosseous
questions.explanation: The median nerve passes between the two heads of pronator teres as it leaves the cubital fossa.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In the cubital fossa, what structure separates the brachial artery from the median cubital vein?
questions.explanation: The bicipital aponeurosis lies over the brachial artery and separates it from the median cubital vein.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In the lower two-thirds of the forearm, what is the ulnar artery's position relative to the ulnar nerve?
options: Posterior to the ulnar nerve within the carpal tunnel
Superficial to the ulnar nerve in the anatomical snuffbox
questions.explanation: The ulnar artery descends lateral to the ulnar nerve in the lower two-thirds of the forearm.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Moving from medial to lateral through the cubital fossa, which sequence of contents is correct?
options: Median nerve, brachial artery, bicipital tendon, radial nerve
Brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve, bicipital tendon
Bicipital tendon, brachial artery, median nerve, radial nerve
Radial nerve, bicipital tendon, brachial artery, median nerve
questions.explanation: The listed order from medial to lateral is median nerve, brachial artery, bicipital tendon, and radial nerve.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: On which structure does the anterior interosseous nerve descend, and which artery accompanies it?
options: On the anterior surface of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery
On the posterior surface of the ulna with the ulnar artery
Within the carpal tunnel with the radial artery
Along the posterior surface of the radius with the posterior interosseous artery
questions.explanation: The slide describes the anterior interosseous nerve descending on the front of the interosseous membrane with the anterior interosseous artery.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: The deep terminal branch of the radial nerve becomes which nerve after piercing the supinator?
questions.explanation: The deep branch pierces the supinator and continues as the posterior interosseous nerve.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which artery accompanies the radial nerve in the spiral groove of the humerus?
questions.explanation: The radial nerve travels in the spiral groove with the profunda brachii artery.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which artery contributes its descending carpal branch to the anterior carpal arch?
questions.explanation: The descending carpal branch of the anterior interosseous artery is one of the contributors to the anterior carpal arch.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which muscle is supplied by the lateral pectoral nerve according to the lecture?
questions.explanation: The lateral pectoral nerve is described as supplying pectoralis major only.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which nerve pierces pectoralis minor before supplying it and then continues to supply pectoralis major?
questions.explanation: The medial pectoral nerve pierces pectoralis minor, supplies it, and then supplies pectoralis major.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which pair forms the arterial anastomosis in front of the medial epicondyle?
options: Superior ulnar collateral and posterior ulnar recurrent arteries
Anterior branch of inferior ulnar collateral and anterior ulnar recurrent arteries
Radial recurrent and posterior descending profunda brachii arteries
Posterior ulnar recurrent and interosseous recurrent arteries
questions.explanation: The anterior branch of the inferior ulnar collateral artery joins the anterior ulnar recurrent artery in front of the medial epicondyle.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which two nerves are exceptions to the brachial-plexus supply of upper-limb skin, as noted in the lecture?
options: Musculocutaneous and medial cutaneous nerves of forearm
questions.explanation: The lecture identifies skin above the deltoid and upper medial arm as supplied by the supraclavicular and intercostobrachial nerves, respectively.
questions.source: The Upper Limb — Nerves, Vessels & Lymphatics — Slides.pdf
questions.topic: Cutaneous innervation of the upper limb
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which non-invasive diagnostic imaging modality is considered the primary initial investigation of choice for suspected lower limb DVT?
questions.explanation: Compression duplex ultrasound is the non-invasive diagnostic investigation of choice for suspected DVT, offering high sensitivity and specificity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 65‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑cm ulcerated lesion on the lower lip. Histology shows nests of malignant epithelial cells with keratin pearl formation. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.explanation: Keratin pearls are characteristic of squamous cell carcinoma of the skin. Basal cell carcinoma shows palisading nuclei, melanoma shows atypical melanocytes, and adenocarcinoma originates from glandular epithelium.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a painless, firm mass in the left upper quadrant. Imaging shows a well‑encapsulated lesion arising from the spleen. Which of the following histological features is most characteristic of a benign splenic hemangioma?
options: A. Sheets of pleomorphic spindle cells with mitotic figures
B. Cystic spaces lined by a single layer of endothelial cells
C. Sheets of small round blue cells with rosette formation
D. Glandular structures with mucin production
questions.explanation: Benign splenic hemangiomas are vascular tumors composed of dilated blood‑filled spaces lined by a single layer of endothelial cells, giving a cystic appearance. The other options describe malignant spindle cell sarcoma, neuroblastoma, and adenocarcinoma, respectively.
questions.source: Basic surgical pathology of splenic lesions
questions.topic: Basic surgical pathology of splenic lesions
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do Transudates differ from Exudates in fluid accumulation (edema/effusions)?
options: Transudates have high protein content (>3 g/dL) and high cellularity due to active inflammation.
Transudates are non-inflammatory ultrafiltrates of plasma with low protein content (<3 g/dL) and few cells, caused by Starling-force imbalances.
Exudates are caused exclusively by left ventricular heart failure and hepatic cirrhosis.
Exudates have a specific gravity of less than 1.012 and lack inflammatory cells entirely.
questions.explanation: Transudates result from Starling-force imbalances (low protein, non-inflammatory), while exudates stem from increased vascular permeability during inflammation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does Apoptosis fundamentally differ from Necrosis regarding energy requirements and inflammatory response?
options: Apoptosis is energy-independent (passive) and triggers severe surrounding inflammation.
Apoptosis is energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) and does not provoke an inflammatory response.
Apoptosis results in massive cellular swelling and cell lysis.
Apoptosis only occurs as a pathological consequence of severe ischemic injury.
questions.explanation: Apoptosis is a regulated, energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) programmed pathway that eliminates cells cleanly without inducing inflammation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury impact organ transplantation and vascular surgery?
options: Releasing the vascular clamp or restoring blood flow delivers oxygen that triggers a burst of ROS and inflammation, paradoxically worsening tissue damage in the graft or limb.
It guarantees 100% immediate cell survival and instant tissue regeneration.
It converts all ischemic tissue into stable fibrous scar tissue within seconds.
It prevents any post-operative thrombosis or edema formation.
questions.explanation: Reperfusion injury is critical in transplantation and vascular clamping because returning blood flow paradoxically exacerbates cellular injury via oxidative stress and inflammation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does the healing process of an Infarct in the brain differ from infarcts in other solid organs (like the heart or kidney)?
options: Brain infarcts heal by forming a dense collagenous fibrous scar.
Brain tissue undergoes liquefactive necrosis which resolves into a fluid-filled cystic cavity rather than a fibrous scar.
Brain infarcts never undergo any structural remodeling or macrophage clearance.
Brain tissue regenerates entirely back to normal functional neurons.
questions.explanation: Unlike solid organs where infarcts are replaced by fibrous scars, liquefactive necrosis in the brain leaves behind a fluid-filled cystic space.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are "Heart Failure Cells" found in chronic passive congestion of the lungs?
options: Hypertrophied cardiac myocytes shed into the pulmonary venous bloodstream
Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages resulting from phagocytosis of extravasated red blood cells in chronic pulmonary congestion
Neoplastic alveolar epithelial cells seen in left-sided valvular tumors
Neutrophils undergoing apoptosis within alveolar exudates
questions.explanation: Left heart failure causes alveolar capillary engorgement and microhemorrhages; macrophages take up iron and become hemosiderin-laden "heart failure cells".
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the possible pathological fates of a newly formed thrombus within a blood vessel?
options: Propagation, embolization, dissolution, organization, and recanalization
Immediate transformation into a transudate effusion
Spontaneous conversion into an active hyperemic vascular bed
Encapsulation by adipose tissue and calcification without local effect
questions.explanation: Thrombi can propagate, dissolve via fibrinolysis, embolize, or undergo organization and recanalization to restore blood flow.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the primary etiologic categories of Shock?
options: Cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic
Ischemic, metabolic, toxic, traumatic, and genetic
questions.explanation: Shock is classified into cardiogenic, hypovolemic, septic, anaphylactic, and neurogenic types based on underlying pathophysiology.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the three components of Virchow's Triad that predispose to pathologic thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability
Platelet depletion, vitamin K deficiency, and excessive fibrinolysis
Increased cardiac output, arterial vasoconstriction, and lymphatic obstruction
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad comprises endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow, and hypercoagulability—all three of which surgery classically contributes to.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What clinical and physiological events characterize the Nonprogressive (Compensated) stage of Shock?
options: Reflex compensatory mechanisms (tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, renal fluid conservation) maintain adequate perfusion of vital organs.
Complete failure of blood pressure with irreversible multi-organ system failure
Massive peripheral vasodilation and warm, flushed extremities without tachycardia
Immediate cessation of all neuroendocrine stress hormone output
questions.explanation: In compensated shock, neurohormonal reflexes sustain blood pressure and perfusion to vital organs before decompensation occurs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What clinical presentation is characteristic of Fat Embolism Syndrome following long-bone fractures or major orthopedic surgery?
options: Immediate onset painless jaundice and hepatomegaly within 30 minutes
A classic triad of petechial rash, dyspnea, and neurologic symptoms developing 1–3 days after injury
Massive upper gastrointestinal hemorrhage from stress ulceration
Spontaneous arterial vasospasm and dry gangrene of all four limbs
questions.explanation: Fat embolism syndrome manifests 1–3 days post-trauma with pulmonary symptoms, neurological impairment, and a characteristic petechial rash.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes Dystrophic Calcification from Metastatic Calcification?
options: Dystrophic calcification occurs in normal, healthy tissues secondary to systemic hypercalcemia.
Dystrophic calcification occurs in dead or damaged tissue in the setting of normal serum calcium levels, whereas metastatic calcification affects normal tissues secondary to hypercalcemia.
Dystrophic calcification only affects the renal cortex and gastric mucosa.
Metastatic calcification is exclusively found inside atherosclerotic plaques and tuberculous scars.
questions.explanation: Dystrophic calcification deposits calcium in injured/necrotic tissue with normal serum calcium, while metastatic calcification requires hypercalcemia affecting normal tissue.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What fundamental hemodynamic difference separates Hyperemia from Congestion?
options: Hyperemia is an active process driven by arteriolar dilation increasing blood inflow, whereas congestion is a passive process caused by impaired venous outflow.
Hyperemia involves cyanotic cold tissues, while congestion produces warm, erythematous tissues.
Hyperemia results exclusively from right heart failure, while congestion results from physical exercise.
Hyperemia is a pathological process, whereas congestion is always a normal physiological response.
questions.explanation: Active hyperemia increases arterial inflow (e.g., exercise, inflammation), whereas passive congestion stems from impaired venous outflow (e.g., heart failure).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What gross and microscopic pathological features define Caseous Necrosis as seen classically in tuberculosis?
options: Bright pink, amorphous protein deposits within blood vessel walls
Friable, white, "cheese-like" central debris surrounded by granulomatous inflammation with Langhans giant cells
Chalky white deposits resulting from enzymatic saponification of fat
Fluid-filled cystic cavities lined by reactive astrocytic glial scars
questions.explanation: Caseous necrosis exhibits a cheese-like gross appearance and acellular granular debris microscopically enclosed within a granulomatous rim.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a Saddle Embolus, and what is its immediate clinical consequence?
options: A small fat globule lodged in a renal glomerulus causing microscopic hematuria
A large thromboembolus straddling the pulmonary artery bifurcation, capable of causing sudden death
An air bubble trapped in the right ventricular outflow tract during laparoscopy
A mural thrombus inside the left atrial appendage
questions.explanation: A saddle embolus occludes the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, leading to acute right heart failure and sudden death.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the crucial clinical distinction between Dry Gangrene and Wet Gangrene in surgical practice?
options: Dry gangrene involves extensive bacterial sepsis, whereas wet gangrene is entirely sterile.
Dry gangrene is caused by ischemia alone with a clear line of demarcation, whereas wet gangrene involves bacterial superinfection, swelling, and high sepsis risk requiring urgent debridement.
Dry gangrene exclusively affects the bowel, while wet gangrene affects only the upper limbs.
Wet gangrene can always be managed expectantly, whereas dry gangrene requires emergency amputation.
questions.explanation: Wet gangrene features bacterial superinfection and carries a high sepsis risk, demanding urgent surgical intervention, unlike dry gangrene.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the earliest morphological manifestation of almost all forms of acute reversible cell injury?
options: Complete dissolution of the plasma membrane
questions.explanation: Cellular swelling is the earliest manifestation of reversible injury, caused by failure of the energy-dependent Na^+/K^+ ATPase pump.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary cellular mechanism underlying cellular aging and reduced physiological reserve in elderly surgical patients?
options: Continuous elongation of chromosomal telomeres beyond normal mitotic thresholds
Progressive accumulation of uncorrected DNA damage, telomere shortening leading to replicative senescence, and misfolded protein buildup
Complete cessation of intracellular reactive oxygen species production
Hypertrophy of all cytoplasmic organelles and increased metabolic efficiency
questions.explanation: Cellular aging reflects accumulated molecular damage, telomere shortening, and protein homeostasis defects, increasing perioperative risk. Part 2: Circulatory Disturbances (Lecture 4)
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary definition of Shock in circulatory pathology?
options: Transient local arterial vasospasm resulting in localized tissue blanching
Systemic hypoperfusion leading to cellular hypoxia and, if uncorrected, cell death
Acute hypertension driven by excessive catecholamine release during surgery
Localized venous congestion due to deep vein thrombosis
questions.explanation: Shock is systemic hypoperfusion causing widespread cellular hypoxia and organ dysfunction.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary pathophysiological driver and surgical significance of Gas Gangrene caused by Clostridium perfringens?
options: Chronic venous stasis leading to painless pedal edema and skin ulceration
Bacterial toxins causing profound muscle necrosis and fermentation producing gas (H_2, CO_2), creating a true surgical emergency with high mortality if debridement is delayed
Immune complex deposition inside small dermal arterioles resulting in fibrinoid vasculitis
Immediate activation of the extrinsic apoptotic pathway via Fas-ligand binding on myocytes
questions.explanation: Gas gangrene is a rapidly progressive, life-threatening infection requiring urgent surgical removal of all dead tissue because antibiotics alone are inadequate.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary surgical rationale for Damage-Control Surgery in severe trauma patients presenting with hemorrhagic shock?
options: To complete all definitive anatomical reconstructions and cosmetic closures in a single 8-hour operation
To prioritize rapid hemorrhage and contamination control over definitive repair, preventing the lethal triad of hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy
To avoid administering any blood products or intravenous crystalloids
To delay all surgical intervention until laboratory clotting parameters are 100% normal
questions.explanation: Damage-control surgery prioritizes arresting bleeding and containing contamination quickly in unstable patients before physiological exhaustion occurs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the single most important determinant of the clinical impact and severity of a Hemorrhage?
options: The anatomical color of the bruising on the skin surface
The total volume of blood lost and the rate at which it is lost
Whether the bleeding is classified as a transudate or an exudate
The patient's resting pulse rate prior to injury
questions.explanation: Volume lost and rate of loss dictate clinical severity; rapid loss of >20% of blood volume risks hemorrhagic shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the underlying biochemical mechanism responsible for the chalky white deposits seen in Fat Necrosis during acute pancreatitis?
options: Deposition of immune complexes and leaked serum fibrin
Saponification, where liberated free fatty acids combine with calcium
Dystrophic calcification secondary to chronic hyperparathyroidism
Bacterial fermentation of subcutaneous adipose tissue lipids
questions.explanation: Leaked pancreatic lipases break down fat, releasing free fatty acids that bind with calcium to form chalky white soap deposits (saponification).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What macroscopic and microscopic features characterize a "Nutmeg Liver" resulting from chronic passive hepatic congestion?
options: Uniform pale yellow discoloration throughout all hepatic lobules due to massive glycogen storage
Centrilobular congestion, hemorrhage, and necrosis with periportal fatty change, creating a mottled red-brown cut surface resembling a nutmeg kernel
Diffuse fibrosis of the portal triads with complete sparing of the central veins
Marked dilation of the hepatic artery branches with ischemic atrophy of Kupffer cells
questions.explanation: Chronic right heart failure causes centrilobular congestion and necrosis alongside periportal steatosis, giving the liver a nutmeg appearance.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What pathological sequence characterizes Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury when blood supply is restored to ischemic tissue?
options: Immediate restoration of normal cellular pH and complete resolution of oxidative stress
A sudden burst of reactive oxygen species (ROS), neutrophil influx, complement activation, and mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening worsening tissue damage
Permanent stabilization of cellular ATP stores and immediate closure of all calcium channels
Conversion of coagulative necrosis into benign fibrous scar tissue within minutes
questions.explanation: Reperfusion floods oxygen-deprived tissue primed for oxidative damage, triggering a massive ROS burst, inflammation, and further cellular injury.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What pathophysiological mechanisms operate in Septic Shock?
options: Primary failure of the cardiac pacemaker node without peripheral vasodilation
Endotoxin and cytokine release causing systemic vasodilation, increased vascular permeability, myocardial depression, and often disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
Acute IgE-mediated bronchospasm without endothelial activation
Complete loss of spinal sympathetic outflow following local anesthetic administration
questions.explanation: Septic shock involves microbial mediators triggering widespread vasodilation, capillary leak, myocardial dysfunction, and coagulopathy.

questions.stem: What percentage of clinical pulmonary emboli originate from deep vein thrombosis in the lower extremities (femoral, popliteal, and iliac veins)?
options: Exactly 100% with no other known sources
questions.explanation: Over 95% of pulmonary thromboemboli originate from deep leg vein thrombi.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What structural features distinguish an Arterial ("White") Thrombus from a Venous ("Red") Thrombus?
options: Arterial thrombi are erythrocyte-rich and form in deep leg vein valve pockets, while venous thrombi are platelet-rich and form on atherosclerotic plaques.
Arterial thrombi are platelet- and fibrin-rich with alternating "Lines of Zahn", whereas venous thrombi are erythrocyte-rich, resembling stagnant clotted blood.
Arterial thrombi never undergo organization or recanalization.
Venous thrombi exclusively cause myocardial infarction and acute stroke.
questions.explanation: Arterial white thrombi are platelet/fibrin-rich with Lines of Zahn at injury sites, while venous red thrombi are erythrocyte-rich clots formed in areas of stasis.

questions.stem: What terminology describes pinpoint hemorrhages measuring 1–2 mm in the skin or mucosa, typically indicative of low platelet count or platelet dysfunction?

questions.stem: Which executioner proteolytic enzymes are central to both the intrinsic and extrinsic pathways of apoptosis?
questions.explanation: Caspases are proteolytic enzymes that act as the main executioners of apoptosis, degrading cellular proteins and DNA.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which four primary physiological mechanisms account for the formation of clinical Edema?
options: Increased vascular hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, and sodium/water retention
Decreased arterial blood pressure, increased plasma albumin synthesis, enhanced renal perfusion, and local vasoconstriction
Primary bone marrow failure, hypercoagulability, endothelial denudation, and stasis
Excessive red blood cell mass, platelet hyperactivity, increased capillary fragility, and rapid thrombolysis
questions.explanation: Edema is governed by Starling forces and fluid regulation: high hydrostatic pressure, low oncotic pressure, lymphatic blockage, and renal salt/water retention.

questions.stem: Which histological sequence accurately describes the nuclear changes of necrosis (cell death)?
questions.explanation: Nuclear necrosis proceeds from pyknosis (shrinkage/condensation), to karyorrhexis (fragmentation), to karyolysis (fading via DNase digestion).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which intracellular event represents the critical "point of no return" that transitions a cell from reversible injury to irreversible injury and cell death?
options: Detachment of ribosomal subunits from the rough endoplasmic reticulum
Severe mitochondrial damage with failure of ATP production and marked Ca^{2+} influx
Reversible cellular (hydropic) swelling due to temporary Na^+/K^+ pump sluggishness
Mild plasma membrane blebbing and blunting of microvilli
questions.explanation: Severe mitochondrial damage, profound ATP depletion, marked calcium influx, and lysosomal rupture constitute the point of no return leading to cell death.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which organs are classically designated as "Shock Organs" displaying characteristic pathological lesions during prolonged systemic hypoperfusion?
options: Kidneys (acute tubular necrosis), Lungs (ARDS/diffuse alveolar damage), Brain (ischemic encephalopathy), Heart, and Gastrointestinal tract
Thyroid gland, skeletal muscles, and skin epidermis exclusively
Gallbladder, spleen, and pancreas with complete sparing of the kidneys
Large conducting arteries and peripheral nerve trunks
questions.explanation: Prolonged shock targets vulnerable organs, producing acute tubular necrosis in kidneys, ARDS in lungs, and ischemic injury in the brain, heart, and gut.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which pattern of necrosis is classically characterized by the preservation of basic tissue architecture ("ghost outlines") for days following ischemic death in solid organs like the heart and kidney?

questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which tissue or organ demonstrates the highest sensitivity and shortest tolerance to complete ischemia (hypoxia)?
options: Brain neurons (tolerate only 3–4 minutes of ischemia)
questions.explanation: Neurons in the central nervous system tolerate only 3–4 minutes of ischemia, whereas myocardium tolerates 20–30 minutes and fibroblasts are more resistant.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why do tissues like the lung and small intestine characteristically develop Red (Hemorrhagic) Infarcts following vascular occlusion?
options: Because they possess a strict end-arterial supply with zero collateral vessels.
Because they feature loose tissue structure or dual blood supplies that permit blood to seep into the necrotic zone from anastomosing channels.
Because their cells are completely immune to hypoxic injury and oxidative stress.
Because venous drainage is always permanently unobstructed.
questions.explanation: Loose tissues and dual blood supplies allow blood to accumulate in the infarcted area, producing a red, hemorrhagic appearance.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why does hypoxic or ischemic cell death in the central nervous system characteristically result in liquefactive necrosis rather than coagulative necrosis?
options: Because the brain has an extensive dual blood supply with abundant collateral anastomoses
Because brain tissue has a high lipid content and scant stroma, and dead cells are completely digested by hydrolytic enzymes
Because neurons lack all forms of intracellular lysosomes and structural proteins
Because the skull prevents any inflammatory cell recruitment into the cranial vault
questions.explanation: The brain undergoes liquefactive necrosis due to high lipid content and scant stroma, where leukocytes and cellular enzymes liquefy the tissue into a viscous mass.

questions.stem: Why does Testicular Torsion represent a surgical emergency regarding circulatory disturbances?
options: It causes immediate systemic anaphylaxis through antigen release.
It causes venous outflow obstruction followed by arterial compromise, leading to a time-critical hemorrhagic (red) infarction of the gonad.
It triggers dry gangrene that can be managed safely with observation alone.
It induces metastatic calcification of the spermatic cord.

Passing medical terminology tests without clinical application
Avoiding all surgical operations in elderly patients

questions.stem: How does the distinction between dry and wet gangrene guide surgical management?
options: Dry gangrene can sometimes be managed expectantly or allowed to auto-amputate, whereas wet gangrene demands urgent surgical debridement or amputation due to high sepsis risk
Both conditions can always be treated with warm saline soaks
Dry gangrene requires immediate emergency amputation within 10 minutes

questions.stem: How does the management of dry gangrene differ fundamentally from wet gangrene in surgical practice?
options: Dry gangrene involves mummification without infection and can often be managed expectantly or allowed to auto-amputate, whereas wet gangrene is a surgical emergency requiring immediate debridement/amputation to prevent fatal sepsis
Both conditions require identical emergency amputation within 1 hour
Neither condition requires any medical or surgical attention
Wet gangrene is managed solely with warm saline

questions.stem: How does the Stress Response Spectrum describe the fate of a normal cell exposed to injurious stimuli?
options: Normal homeostasis → Adaptation → Reversible Injury (stimulus removed, recovery possible) → Irreversible Injury (necrosis or apoptosis cell death)
Normal homeostasis → Immediate death without adaptation
Reversible injury always leads to cancer

questions.stem: In which clinical condition is Dystrophic Calcification commonly found by surgeons?

Blood serum of normal healthy young adults

Pyknosis, Karyorrhexis, Karyolysis, Apoptosis, and Necrosis

Dry: Caused by bacterial infection; Wet: Caused by ischemia alone

questions.stem: What are the key microscopic and macroscopic morphological features of Apoptosis?
options: Cell swelling, membrane disruption, and massive acute inflammation
Cell shrinkage, chromatin condensation, membrane blebbing, formation of apoptotic bodies, and phagocytosis by macrophages WITHOUT inflammation
Liquefaction into pus and neutrophil infiltration
questions.explanation: Apoptotic cells fragment into membrane-wrapped bodies exposing 'eat-me' signals (phosphatidylserine), ensuring prompt macrophage clearance without tissue inflammation.

questions.stem: What are the two principal signaling pathways of Apoptosis?

questions.stem: What causes intracellular accumulation of Glycogen, and in which conditions is it classically seen?
options: Abnormal glucose metabolism, such as Diabetes Mellitus and Glycogen Storage Diseases
questions.explanation: Impaired glucose processing leads to excessive glycogen vacuolization in renal tubular epithelium, liver cells, and beta cells.

questions.stem: What causes the 'chalky white' appearance of fat necrosis grossly in acute pancreatitis?

questions.stem: What clinical consequence arises from failure of the Na+/K+ ATPase pump during early reversible ischemic cell injury?
options: Intracellular accumulation of sodium and water, leading to acute hydropic cellular swelling
questions.explanation: Loss of active ionic pumping collapses osmotic balance, swelling the cell body and cytoplasmic organelles.

questions.stem: What defines Apoptosis as a form of cell death?
options: Uncontrolled, energy-independent destruction with severe inflammation
A regulated, energy-dependent (ATP-requiring) programmed cell death pathway that eliminates unwanted or damaged cells without provoking inflammation
Accidental cell bursting caused by bacterial toxins
Swelling and rupture of plasma membranes
questions.explanation: Apoptosis utilizes an active enzymatic cascade to neatly dismantle cells into membrane-bound bodies engulfed by macrophages.

questions.stem: What defines Gangrenous Necrosis in a surgical context?
options: A distinct primary pattern of cell death caused directly by viruses
Clinical term for ischemic death of tissue (typically involving a lower limb or bowel) complicated by secondary bacterial infection and putrefaction

questions.stem: What distinguishes microscopic findings in an abscess (liquefactive necrosis)?

Amorphous debris, abundant neutrophils, and complete loss of cellular outlines

questions.stem: What distinguishes the microscopic appearance of coagulative necrosis?

questions.stem: What factors determine whether an injured cell adapts, recovers, or dies?

The operating room temperature and humidity
questions.explanation: Vulnerable myocardial cells infarct rapidly under ischemia, whereas robust fibroblasts tolerate transient hypoxia much better.

questions.stem: What histological and gross features characterize Fat Necrosis?
options: Destruction of adipose tissue by lipases or trauma, liberating free fatty acids that combine with calcium to form chalky white deposits ('saponification')
Liquefaction of the brain into pus
Caseous white granulomas in the lung

questions.stem: What histological and morphological features distinguish Apoptosis from Necrosis on H&E tissue examination?
options: Apoptosis shows single cell shrinkage, condensed chromatin, and apoptotic bodies without inflammation; Necrosis shows groups of swollen cells, membrane rupture, nuclear pyknosis/karyolysis, and acute inflammation
Apoptosis shows massive pus and neutrophil infiltration
Necrosis shows single cell shrinkage without inflammation
Both appear identical under the microscope

questions.stem: What is Caseous Necrosis, and which infectious organism is its classic hallmark?

Friable, white, 'cheese-like' appearance in the center of granulomas caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Fibrinoid deposition in blood vessels caused by hypertension
Saponification of fat caused by pancreatic enzymes

questions.stem: What is Cellular Aging, and what are its primary molecular drivers?
options: Progressive accumulation of cellular and molecular damage over time leading to decreased functional capacity, driven by DNA damage accumulation, telomere shortening, defective protein homeostasis, and mitochondrial dysfunction
Acute bacterial infection acquired in the operating theatre
Rapid cellular regeneration in response to hormones

Calcium deposition in dead, damaged, or necrotic tissues; serum calcium levels are NORMAL
Calcium deposition in healthy bone; serum calcium is decreased
Calcium loss from the skeleton; serum calcium is zero

Deposition of calcium in heart valves
Accumulation of glycogen in the brain

Rapidly progressive, life-threatening soft tissue infection caused by Clostridium perfringens producing gas (H2, CO2) and severe muscle necrosis
Fungal infection of the lung caused by Aspergillus

questions.stem: What is Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury, and in which surgical scenarios is it particularly critical?

Tissue injury that paradoxically intensifies when blood supply is restored to ischemic tissue, driven by a ROS burst and neutrophil influx; critical in organ transplantation, vascular clamp release, cardiopulmonary bypass, and tourniquet use
Injury caused exclusively by bacterial superinfection

questions.stem: What is Lipofuscin, and why is it frequently referred to as the 'wear-and-tear' pigment?

An iron storage complex found in hemochromatosis

questions.stem: What is Metastatic Calcification, and what is its primary underlying systemic cause?

Calcium deposition in necrotic heart valves with normal serum calcium
Spread of bone cancer to visceral organs

questions.stem: What is the cellular hallmark of Reversible Injury that allows full recovery if the stimulus is removed?

Permanent replacement by fibrous scar tissue

options: Denaturation of structural proteins and enzymes preserves basic tissue architecture (ghost outlines of cells), classic for ischemic death in solid organs like heart, kidney, and spleen
Cheese-like friable white appearance caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis

It is a mitochondrial enzyme that synthesizes ATP
It causes coagulative necrosis in the heart

It binds calcium to form soap deposits
It synthesizes glycogen in the liver

Elderly patients have identical physiological reserve to neonates
Wound healing is accelerated in elderly patients
Aging has zero impact on surgical outcomes

It replaces the need for anesthesia
It predicts the patient's insurance coverage

Pathology is only used for billing purposes
Rejection is diagnosed exclusively by blood pressure

questions.stem: What triggers the INTRINSIC (mitochondrial) pathway of apoptosis?

Binding of external Fas ligand to cell surface death receptors

Nuclear membrane only (no other membranes affected)

Severe mitochondrial damage with failure of ATP generation and extensive plasma membrane damage
Mild chromatin clumping in the nucleus

Uncontrolled, energy-independent cell death occurring in living tissue that triggers an inflammatory response and is always pathologic

Embryogenesis, hormone-dependent tissue involution, and immune cell turnover/selection

questions.stem: Why do intracellular accumulations of lipids (steatosis) occur predominantly in the liver?

Because the liver lacks blood vessels
Because the liver is composed entirely of adipose tissue
Because hepatocytes do not require ATP

questions.stem: Why does hypoxia in the Central Nervous System (CNS/brain) result in Liquefactive Necrosis rather than Coagulative Necrosis?
options: Because brain tissue lacks blood vessels
Because brain tissue has high lipid content, scant stroma, and abundant hydrolytic enzymes that rapidly digest dead neural tissue into a viscous liquid mass
Because the brain undergoes caseous necrosis
Because neurons have rigid cell walls

questions.stem: Why is Gas Gangrene considered a true surgical emergency where antibiotics alone are inadequate?
options: Because antibiotics cannot penetrate blood vessels, and necrotic tissue packed with bacteria and gas requires urgent, aggressive surgical debridement or amputation to prevent rapid mortality
Because gas gangrene resolves spontaneously within 24 hours
Because antibiotics neutralize bacterial gas bubbles instantly
Because surgery is strictly contraindicated in clostridial infections

questions.stem: Why is understanding Ischemia-Reperfusion Injury critical during vascular clamp release or organ transplantation?
options: Because restoring blood flow generates a massive oxidative burst of ROS and inflammation that can damage the newly reperfused organ or cause systemic reperfusion syndrome
Because blood flow restoration has zero physiological impact
Because clamps prevent all cell death

questions.stem: What pathological process marks the transition from compensated shock to decompensated shock?
options: Shift to anaerobic cellular metabolism, worsening metabolic acidosis, and failing organ perfusion.
questions.explanation: Decompensated shock occurs when compensatory mechanisms fail, leading to anaerobic metabolism, lactic acidosis, and falling blood pressure.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of progressive dysphagia to solids and weight loss. Endoscopic ultrasound shows a 4 cm hypoechoic mass in the proximal stomach. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology reveals sheets of cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, prominent nucleoli, and a high mitotic rate. Which of the following immunohistochemical stains is most likely to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.explanation: The cytology is characteristic of a poorly differentiated gastric adenocarcinoma. Cytokeratin 7 is typically expressed in gastric epithelium and is the most useful marker to confirm an adenocarcinoma of gastric origin. Cytokeratin 20 is usually negative in gastric cancers, while chromogranin A and synaptophysin are neuroendocrine markers that would be positive only if the tumour were a neuroendocrine carcinoma.

questions.stem: How do Exudates structurally and biochemically differ from Transudates in fluid accumulation?
options: Exudates have a low protein content (<3\text{ g/dL}) and specific gravity (<1.012) due to non-inflammatory Starling-force imbalances.
Exudates are inflammatory fluids with high protein content (>3\text{ g/dL}), specific gravity (>1.020), and a turbid appearance resulting from increased vascular permeability.
Transudates contain high cellularity rich in neutrophils and are caused by localized bacterial infection.
Transudates have a specific gravity exceeding 1.020 and a turbid gross appearance.
questions.explanation: Exudates are protein-rich (>3 g/dL) inflammatory fluids with high specific gravity (>1.020), while transudates are non-inflammatory fluid shifts.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do the granulomas of Sarcoidosis and Crohn's Disease differ histologically from Tuberculosis?
options: They display central caseous necrosis identical to tuberculosis.
They are non-caseating granulomas lacking central necrosis.
They contain abundant neutrophils and frank purulent abscesses.
They consist exclusively of plasma cells and B-lymphocytes without macrophages.
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis and Crohn's disease present with non-caseating granulomas (no central necrosis), unlike caseating tuberculous granulomas.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What common surgical complication arises from chronic inflammation producing excessive collagen deposition and tissue remodeling in conditions like Crohn's disease?
options: Spontaneous resolution of all transmural pathology
Acute fulminant arterial hemorrhage from mesenteric vessels
Widespread mucosal epithelial hyperplasia without scarring
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation leads to fibrosis and scarring, causing strictures and obstruction (e.g., in Crohn's disease).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What histological and cellular features characterize Chronic Inflammation?
options: Predominance of short-lived neutrophils, minimal tissue destruction, and immediate complete resolution
Infiltration by mononuclear inflammatory cells (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells), ongoing tissue destruction, and simultaneous repair via fibrosis and angiogenesis
Massive deposition of immune complexes inside vessel walls producing fibrinoid necrosis exclusively
Rapid fluid accumulation with low protein transudates and absent cellular infiltrate
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation features mononuclear infiltrates, persistent tissue destruction, and concurrent angiogenesis and fibrotic healing.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the correct chronological sequence of leukocyte recruitment steps during the cellular phase of acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Leukocytes first marginate to the periphery, roll via selectins, adhere via integrins, cross via diapedesis (PECAM-1), and migrate via chemotaxis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the recognized long-term oncological link between chronic inflammation and malignant transformation (e.g., Helicobacter pylori and gastric cancer)?
options: Chronic inflammation reduces cellular turnover and protects DNA integrity.
Chronic inflammation generates mutagenic reactive oxygen species (ROS) and pro-inflammatory cytokines that drive mutagenesis and cancer risk.
Chronic inflammation causes immediate apoptosis of all precancerous cells.
Chronic inflammation induces permanent hypoplasia of the gastric mucosa.
questions.explanation: Persistent chronic inflammation promotes carcinogenesis through mutagenic ROS and cytokine release (e.g., H. pylori leading to gastric adenocarcinoma/MALT lymphoma).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the required clinical management for a localized surgical Abscess containing pus (neutrophils and debris)?
options: High-dose systemic antibiotic monotherapy is completely sufficient to resolve the collection.
Surgical drainage is mandatory because antibiotics alone cannot resolve a walled-off abscess collection.
Immediate anti-inflammatory corticosteroid administration to induce resolution.
Expectant observation without intervention, as abscesses always resolve via complete restoration.
questions.explanation: Abscesses are localized pus collections walled off by fibrous tissue; antibiotics treat surrounding cellulitis, but the collection itself requires surgical drainage.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What pathological triad constitutes a Surgical Site Infection (SSI) suppurative infiltrate?
options: Lymphocytes, caseous necrosis, and foreign body giant cells
Epithelioid macrophages, plasma cells, and dense collagen
Foamy macrophages, cholesterol clefts, and hemosiderin
questions.explanation: Acute suppurative inflammation (pus) consists of neutrophils, fibrin, and bacteria.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What primary physiological purpose does the acute inflammatory vascular and cellular response serve?
options: To permanently destroy vascular integrity and induce systemic hypovolemic shock
To isolate, destroy the causative agent, and repair tissue damage
To replace all normal parenchymal cells with adipose tissue
To suppress all immune cell recruitment and prevent antibody production
questions.explanation: Inflammation is a protective response designed to eliminate harmful agents and initiate tissue repair.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What systemic complication is specifically associated with prolonged chronic inflammatory diseases due to extracellular deposition of AA-type protein fibrils?

questions.stem: Which cellular component serves as the primary "first responder" arriving within 6 to 24 hours at the site of acute inflammation?

questions.stem: Which chemical mediators are specifically highlighted in the lecture as being primarily responsible for causing pain and vasodilation during acute inflammation?

questions.stem: Which morphological pattern of chronic inflammation is characterized by foamy macrophages accumulating lipids and serves as a surgically important mimic of malignancy (e.g., in xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis)?

questions.stem: Which type of multinucleated giant cell is classically associated with caseating granulomas in Tuberculosis?

Langhans giant cells (horseshoe-shaped peripheral nuclei arrangement)
Touton giant cells with lipid-laden borders

questions.stem: Why is surveillance colonoscopy recommended for patients with long-standing Inflammatory Bowel Disease (IBD)?
options: To monitor for stricture formation and remove foreign body sutures
Because long-standing chronic inflammation in IBD carries an increased long-term risk of colorectal cancer
To evaluate the efficacy of acute neutrophil degranulation inhibitors
To prevent the development of caseating granulomas in the colon
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation in IBD is pro-carcinogenic, necessitating regular colonoscopic surveillance for colorectal cancer.

questions.stem: Histological identification of foamy, lipid-laden macrophages defines which morphological pattern of chronic inflammation, known as an important surgical mimic of malignancy?

It is surgically critical because it forms mass lesions that clinically and radiologically mimic carcinoma (e.g., xanthogranulomatous pyelonephritis and xanthogranulomatous cholecystitis).

questions.stem: How does an Exudate differ biochemically and physically from a Transudate?
options: Exudates have low protein (<3 g/dL) and clear appearance due to hydrostatic force imbalances
Exudates have high protein (>3 g/dL), high specific gravity (>1.020), and a turbid appearance due to increased vascular permeability from inflammation
Transudates have high specific gravity (>1.020) and are rich in inflammatory neutrophils
Both fluids have identical protein concentrations but differ in temperature
questions.explanation: Exudates are turbid, inflammatory fluids formed by increased vascular permeability, featuring protein >3 g/dL and specific gravity >1.020. Transudates are clear ultrafiltrates caused by hydrostatic or oncotic pressure imbalances without significant inflammation, featuring protein <3 g/dL and specific gravity <1.012.
