questions.stem: Multinucleated giant cells with haphazardly scattered nuclei arranged throughout their cytoplasm are characteristic of which granulomatous process?
options: Foreign body reaction (e.g., around surgical sutures or mesh)
questions.explanation: Foreign body giant cells contain nuclei scattered haphazardly throughout the cytoplasm and form around non-digestible exogenously introduced materials such as surgical sutures, synthetic mesh, or prosthetic hardware. Langhans giant cells have nuclei arranged in a peripheral horseshoe arc.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Prolonged, severe chronic inflammatory disease carries a risk for developing which systemic protein accumulation disorder?
questions.explanation: Persistent long-standing chronic inflammation causes sustained hepatic synthesis of Serum Amyloid A (SAA), which can deposit in tissues as insoluble fibrillar deposits, causing secondary (AA-type) amyloidosis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Transmigration of leukocytes through endothelial cell junctions (diapedesis) is primarily mediated by which adhesion molecule?
questions.explanation: Diapedesis (passage of leukocytes across the vascular basement membrane and endothelial junctions) is mediated primarily via PECAM-1 (CD31).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does a pathology report reading "acute suppurative inflammation with abscess formation" indicate regarding the specimen's cellular contents?
options: Mononuclear cell infiltrate dominated by plasma cells and macrophages
Abundant polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs), cellular debris, and bacteria (pus)
Epithelioid histiocytes and non-caseating giant cells
Avascular fibrous scar tissue with low cellularity
questions.explanation: Acute suppurative inflammation is defined pathologically by pus formation, which consists of dead and dying neutrophils (PMNs), liquefied cellular debris, fibrin, and bacteria.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the correct chronological sequence of leukocyte recruitment steps from the vascular lumen to the site of tissue injury?
questions.explanation: Leukocyte recruitment follows a strict sequential pathway: (1) Margination (leukocytes move to vessel periphery), (2) Rolling (selectin-mediated), (3) Adhesion (integrin-mediated), (4) Diapedesis (transmigration via PECAM-1), and (5) Chemotaxis (migration along chemical gradients).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the defining clinical management rule for a localized surgical Abscess?
options: It resolves completely with high-dose intravenous systemic antibiotic monotherapy
It requires surgical incision and drainage because antibiotics alone cannot penetrate and resolve a walled-off pus collection
It requires immediate anti-inflammatory steroid injections into the cavity
It should be observed expectantly as neutrophils auto-digest the wall within 48 hours
questions.explanation: An abscess is a localized collection of pus (PMNs + necrotic debris) surrounded by a dense fibrous wall. Because systemic blood flow cannot penetrate the central necrotic core, antibiotics treat surrounding cellulitis but cannot resolve the collection itself; surgical drainage is mandatory.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the established pathophysiological link connecting long-standing chronic mucosal inflammation to malignant transformation (such as H. pylori and gastric cancer)?
options: Persistent acute neutrophilic degranulation destroys all basement membranes
Chronic inflammation causes sustained release of mutagenic Reactive Oxygen Species (ROS) and pro-inflammatory cytokines, driving genomic instability
Chronic inflammation causes immediate apoptosis of precancerous stem cells
Mononuclear cells synthesize direct oncogenic viral particles
questions.explanation: Prolonged chronic inflammation generates high local concentrations of mutagenic ROS and cytokines that promote cellular proliferation, inhibit apoptosis, and induce DNA mutations. Classic clinical examples include H. pylori leading to gastric adenocarcinoma/MALT lymphoma and long-standing IBD leading to colorectal cancer.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the practical clinical "rule of thumb" when evaluating a surgical biopsy containing caseating granulomatous inflammation?
options: It represents Sarcoidosis until proven otherwise
A caseating granuloma is Tuberculosis (TB) until proven otherwise
It is a benign reaction to suture material requiring no follow-up
questions.explanation: A cardinal rule for surgical trainees dictates that finding a caseating granuloma on histology must be considered Tuberculosis (TB) until proven otherwise. Non-caseating granulomas raise differential diagnoses including sarcoidosis, Crohn's disease, or foreign body reaction.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What microscopic combination defines a Tuberculosis granuloma on surgical biopsy?
options: Non-caseating central matrix enclosed by foreign body giant cells
Central caseating necrosis surrounded by epithelioid macrophages and Langhans giant cells with peripheral horseshoe-arranged nuclei
Foamy lipid macrophages surrounding cholesterol clefts
Neutrophilic abscess surrounded by a thin endothelial wall
questions.explanation: Tuberculosis produces caseating granulomas (central amorphous pink acellular debris) surrounded by epithelioid macrophages, lymphocytes, and Langhans giant cells (characterized by horseshoe-shaped peripheral nuclei).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What pathognomonic triad defines Chronic Inflammation?
options: Neutrophilic infiltration, vasodilation, and rapid tissue resolution
Infiltration by mononuclear inflammatory cells, ongoing tissue destruction, and simultaneous attempts at repair (fibrosis and angiogenesis)
Complete absence of immune cells, vascular thrombosis, and liquefactive necrosis
Serous fluid effusion, fever, and leukocytosis
questions.explanation: Chronic inflammation is a prolonged response (weeks to years) characterized by three simultaneous processes: (1) mononuclear cell infiltration (macrophages, lymphocytes, plasma cells), (2) persistent tissue destruction, and (3) repair via fibrosis and angiogenesis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which arachidonic acid metabolite derived from the lipoxygenase pathway acts as a potent chemoattractant for leukocyte recruitment?
questions.explanation: The cyclooxygenase (COX) pathway yields P G E 2 ​ and P G I 2 ​ (mediating pain, fever, and vasodilation), whereas the lipoxygenase pathway yields L T B 4 ​ , a potent chemotactic factor for neutrophils.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which cell type acts as the central orchestrator of chronic inflammation, executing phagocytosis, antigen presentation, and release of fibrogenic cytokines like T GF − β ?
questions.explanation: Macrophages are the central orchestrators of chronic inflammation. They perform phagocytosis, present antigens to CD4+ T-cells, release cytokines, and activate tissue repair and fibrosis via growth factors such as T GF − β .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which cell type acts as the principal "first responder" in acute inflammation, arriving within 6 to 24 hours at the site of injury?
questions.explanation: Polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) are the primary first responders (arriving within 6–24 hours). They execute phagocytosis, oxidative burst ( H 2 ​ O 2 ​ , HOCl), and degranulation, and form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) before undergoing apoptosis within hours to form pus.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which chemical mediators are specifically responsible for inducing pain (dolor) during the acute inflammatory response?
options: Prostaglandin E 2 ​ ( P G E 2 ​ ) and Bradykinin
Leukotriene B 4 ​ ( L T B 4 ​ ) and Complement C 3 a
Interleukin-1 β ( I L − 1 β ) and Tumor Necrosis Factor- α ( T N F − α )
questions.explanation: Redness (rubor) and heat (calor) are driven by vasodilation and increased blood flow; swelling (tumor) is caused by edema from increased vascular permeability; pain (dolor) is specifically mediated by P G E 2 ​ and bradykinin.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which class of cell adhesion molecules mediates the firm attachment (adhesion) of leukocytes to endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1 during acute inflammation?
questions.explanation: Leukocyte rolling along the endothelial surface is mediated by selectins, whereas firm adhesion is mediated by leukocyte integrins binding to endothelial ICAM-1 and VCAM-1.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which cytokine released by activated Th1 CD4+ T-lymphocytes is essential for driving macrophage activation and transformation into epithelioid histiocytes during granuloma formation?
options: Interferon- γ ( I F N − γ )
Tumor Necrosis Factor- α ( T N F − α )
questions.explanation: In granulomatous inflammation, antigen-presenting macrophages activate Th1 CD4+ T-cells, which secrete I F N − γ . I F N − γ induces macrophage activation, epithelioid cell transformation, and subsequent cell fusion into multinucleated giant cells.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which cytokines released by activated tissue macrophages are primarily responsible for driving the systemic acute-phase response and fever?
options: Interleukin-4 ( I L − 4 ) and Interleukin-10 ( I L − 10 )
Interleukin-1 β ( I L − 1 β ) and Tumor Necrosis Factor- α ( T N F − α )
Transforming Growth Factor- β ( T GF − β ) and Interferon- γ ( I F N − γ )
questions.explanation: Macrophage-derived I L − 1 β and T N F − α serve as key systemic cytokines that induce pyrexia (fever) and stimulate liver synthesis of acute-phase reactant proteins.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which histological features characterize the granulomas seen in transmural bowel resections of patients with Crohn's Disease?
options: Central caseating necrosis with Langhans giant cells
Non-caseating granulomas with foreign-body type giant cells
Suppurative neutrophilic micro-abscesses with Schaumann bodies
Abundant foam cells filled with lipid droplets
questions.explanation: Unlike tuberculosis, Crohn's disease produces non-caseating granulomas (lacking central necrosis) containing foreign-body type giant cells within the transmural layers of the intestinal wall.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How are Biological Markers categorized according to their specific clinical roles?
questions.explanation: Biomarkers serve distinct clinical roles as diagnostic, prognostic, predictive, or monitoring tools.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How are Grade, Stage, and Biomarkers integrated in clinical oncology decision-making?
options: They are evaluated in isolation, where stage alone determines all medical and surgical treatment protocols.
They answer distinct questions (aggressiveness, spread, molecular profile) and are integrated together to form an individualized prognosis and multi-modal treatment plan.
Biomarkers completely replace histological grading and anatomical staging in modern practice.
Grading is utilized exclusively for epidemiological statistics rather than patient care.
questions.explanation: Optimal prognosis and personalized treatment planning require integrating grade, stage, and biological markers together.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What advantage does a "Liquid Biopsy" (measuring ctDNA or CTCs) offer over traditional tissue biopsy?
options: It provides exact 3D architectural tissue orientation and surgical margin status.
It is minimally invasive, easily repeatable over time, and captures tumor heterogeneity across multiple metastatic sites.
It completely replaces the need for any microscopic pathology or clinical staging.
It has 100% specificity with zero risk of false-positive elevations.
questions.explanation: Liquid biopsies are minimally invasive, repeatable, and overcome single-site tissue biopsy limitations regarding tumor heterogeneity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the primary limitations associated with serum tumor markers in clinical oncology?
options: 100% sensitivity and specificity across all early-stage cancers.
Limited sensitivity and specificity, potential false positives from benign conditions, and inability to serve as standalone diagnostic tools.
Complete instability when exposed to standard laboratory storage temperatures.
Inability to be measured via automated blood analyzers.
questions.explanation: Tumor markers have limited sensitivity/specificity and can be elevated in benign states, meaning they support but do not replace histological diagnosis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the three primary pathways or routes of Metastatic Spread?
options: Direct seeding of body cavities, lymphatic spread, and hematogenous spread.
Perineural tracking, trans-epithelial migration, and airborne transmission.
Arterial embolism, ductal reflux, and direct osmotic diffusion.
Superficial ulceration, direct mechanical pressure, and thermal conduction.
questions.explanation: Malignancies spread via direct seeding in body cavities, lymphatic channels (favored by carcinomas), or blood vessels (favored by sarcomas).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What biological phenomenon explains why certain tumors preferentially metastasize to specific target organs (e.g., prostate cancer to bone)?
options: Simple anatomical blood flow patterns alone.
Organotropism driven by specific adhesion molecule expression and a favorable "seed and soil" microenvironment.
Complete absence of capillary beds in non-target organs.
Active mechanical trapping of large cell clusters inside renal glomeruli.
questions.explanation: Organotropism dictates metastatic destination based on molecular interactions between tumor cells ("seed") and target organ microenvironments ("soil").
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What clinical implication is associated with KRAS mutations in Colorectal Carcinoma?
options: They predict high sensitivity and favorable response to anti-EGFR antibody therapy.
They predict primary resistance to anti-EGFR antibody therapy.
They guarantee complete cure following surgical enucleation alone.
They convert adenocarcinoma into a benign adenoma.
questions.explanation: KRAS mutations confer resistance to anti-EGFR antibody therapies in colorectal cancer management.
questions.topic: Surgical oncology: KRAS and anti-EGFR resistance
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What clinical significance is associated with Paraneoplastic Syndromes in oncology?
options: They are caused exclusively by direct physical compression of local nerve roots.
They may be the first clinical clue to an occult malignancy and can occur even when tumors are too small to cause local symptoms.
They only occur in patients with benign adenomas.
They eliminate the need for any surgical staging or histological grading.
questions.explanation: Paraneoplastic syndromes represent remote systemic effects of tumors that can precede local symptoms and signal occult cancer.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What components make up the core TNM Staging Classification framework?
options: Total tumor weight (T), number of mitoses (N), and margin status (M).
Size/local extent of primary tumor (T), regional lymph node involvement (N), and presence of distant metastasis (M).
Tissue differentiation (T), necrosis percentage (N), and vascular invasion (M).
Translocation status (T), nuclear grade (N), and molecular profile (M).
questions.explanation: The TNM system assesses primary tumor extent (T), regional lymph node spread (N), and distant metastasis (M).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What constitutes Cancer Cachexia, and how does it manifest clinically?
options: Rapid weight gain and massive adipose tissue accumulation around visceral organs.
Progressive weight loss, muscle atrophy, and weakness disproportionate to tumor bulk.
Selective loss of appetite resulting purely from mechanical esophageal obstruction.
Acute fluid retention and generalized pitting edema identical to nephrotic syndrome.
questions.explanation: Cancer cachexia is a systemic wasting syndrome characterized by profound weight loss and weakness out of proportion to tumor size.
questions.topic: Surgical nutrition and oncology: cancer cachexia
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a true Neoplasm from a Hamartoma?
options: A hamartoma is a malignant mesenchymal tumor with high mitotic activity.
A hamartoma is a developmental malformation composed of disorganized but mature native tissue, not a true neoplasm.
A hamartoma arises from more than one germ cell layer via totipotent cells.
Hamartomas always metastasize exclusively via hematogenous routes.
questions.explanation: Hamartomas represent localized developmental malformations of mature native tissue rather than true autonomous neoplasms.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes Clinical Staging (cTNM) from Pathologic Staging (pTNM)?
options: Clinical staging relies on physical exams, imaging, and pre-treatment biopsy, whereas pathologic staging relies on histologic examination of surgically resected tissues.
Clinical staging is only performed post-mortem during autopsy.
Pathologic staging never evaluates regional lymph nodes or surgical margins.
Clinical staging is completely independent of the TNM framework.
questions.explanation: Clinical staging guides initial pre-treatment planning using exams and imaging, while pathologic staging provides precise data from resected specimens.
questions.topic: Surgical oncology: clinical and pathological staging
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes Proto-oncogenes from Tumor Suppressor Genes in cancer pathogenesis?
options: Proto-oncogenes undergo loss-of-function mutations, while tumor suppressor genes undergo gain-of-function mutations.

Proto-oncogenes undergo gain-of-function mutations converting them into hyperactive drivers of proliferation, whereas tumor suppressor genes undergo loss-of-function mutations removing normal cell cycle brakes.
Proto-oncogenes regulate DNA repair exclusively, while tumor suppressor genes control cellular respiration.
Tumor suppressors are viral genes, while proto-oncogenes are strictly inherited.
questions.explanation: Oncogenes act via gain-of-function (driving growth), while tumor suppressors require loss-of-function (removing brakes).
questions.topic: Pathology: oncogenes and tumor suppressor genes
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does an elevated Ki-67 index signify in histopathological evaluation?
options: Complete absence of cellular proliferation and permanent cell cycle arrest.
The proliferation index, estimating the growth fraction of the tumor.
Positive hormonal receptor status for endocrine-responsive breast cancer.
The presence of heavy metastatic tumor burden in regional bone marrow.
questions.explanation: Ki-67 is a proliferation marker that estimates the active growth fraction of a tumor cell population.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What functional gene classes are central to the molecular basis of carcinogenesis?
options: Structural collagen genes, keratin genes, and hemoglobin genes.
Proto-oncogenes (oncogenes), tumor suppressor genes, DNA repair genes, and apoptosis-regulating genes.
Ribosomal RNA genes and mitochondrial transfer genes.
Osmoregulatory genes and digestive enzyme genes.
questions.explanation: Cancer arises from genetic mutations affecting oncogenes, tumor suppressors, DNA repair pathways, and apoptosis regulators.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the clinical utility of a Sentinel Lymph Node Biopsy?
options: To completely remove all lymphatic chains in the body to prevent primary tumor initiation.
To identify and assess the first-draining lymph node for regional spread with significantly less morbidity than full nodal dissection.
To measure circulating serum PSA and CEA levels pre-operatively.
To deliver targeted radiation directly to distant bone metastases.
questions.explanation: Sentinel lymph node biopsy identifies the initial draining node to stage regional spread while avoiding the morbidity of full dissections.
questions.topic: Surgical oncology: sentinel lymph node biopsy
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the difference between Direct-acting and Indirect-acting Chemical Carcinogens?
options: Direct-acting agents require metabolic activation in the liver, while indirect-acting agents do not.
Direct-acting agents require no metabolic conversion to be active, whereas indirect-acting agents (procarcinogens) require metabolic activation.
Direct-acting agents only cause benign tumors, while indirect-acting agents cause sarcomas.
Direct-acting agents are natural plant alkaloids, while indirect-acting agents are physical radiation forms.
questions.explanation: Direct-acting carcinogens act directly without conversion, whereas procarcinogens (indirect-acting) require metabolic activation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary histological and clinical difference between Tumor Grade and Tumor Stage?
options: Grade measures anatomic extent of disease, whereas stage measures cellular differentiation under the microscope.
Grade measures histologic differentiation and cellular aggressiveness, whereas stage measures the anatomic extent of disease (tumor size, nodal spread, and metastasis).
Grade is determined solely by blood serum tumor markers, whereas stage requires genetic sequencing.
Grade and stage are interchangeable terms used exclusively for staging lymphomas.
questions.explanation: Grade describes how malignant cells look under the microscope (differentiation), while stage describes how far the malignancy has spread anatomically.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the single most reliable feature distinguishing malignant from benign neoplasms?
options: High mitotic rate and cellular pleomorphism.
The presence of metastasis (secondary tumor deposits discontinuous with the primary).
Elevated serum CA-125 and CEA levels.
Large primary tumor size exceeding 10 centimeters.
questions.explanation: Metastasis formation is the absolute hallmark and most reliable feature differentiating malignancy from benign tumors.
questions.topic: Pathology: metastasis as evidence of malignancy
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the single strongest predictor of prognosis for the majority of solid tumors?
questions.explanation: Staging measures the anatomic extent of disease at diagnosis, making it the single strongest predictor of prognosis for solid tumors.
questions.topic: Surgical oncology: prognostic significance of stage
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What mechanism drives Local Invasion in malignant tumors compared to benign tumors?
options: Benign tumors form rigid fibrous capsules and push against tissue, whereas malignant tumors lack capsules, destroy surrounding tissue, and infiltrate along tissue planes, nerves, and vessels.
Malignant tumors rely exclusively on rapid encapsulation to compress adjacent organs.
Benign tumors actively secrete matrix metalloproteinases to degrade basement membranes.
Malignant invasion is driven by increased intercellular adhesion mediated by overexpressed E-cadherin.
questions.explanation: Expansile growth with a capsule characterizes benign tumors, while infiltrative growth without a capsule defines malignancy.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What primary limitation affects the reliability of Tumor Grading in clinical practice?
options: Tumor heterogeneity, interobserver subjectivity, and small biopsy sampling limitations.
Complete absence of any nuclear atypia in high-grade sarcomas.
Inability of grading systems to ever correlate with patient survival.
Mandatory reliance on circulating liquid biopsies rather than tissue slides.
questions.explanation: Grading is limited by interobserver variability, tumor heterogeneity, and sampling errors from small needle biopsies.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What scoring system is standard practice for grading Prostate Carcinoma based on architectural growth patterns?
questions.explanation: Prostate carcinoma utilizes the Gleason score based on the architectural growth patterns of the two most prevalent areas.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What specific type of DNA damage is induced by Ultraviolet (UV) radiation leading to skin carcinogenesis?
options: Double-strand DNA breaks repaired by homologous recombination.
questions.explanation: UV radiation causes DNA damage via pyrimidine dimer formation, linked to basal cell, squamous cell, and melanoma skin cancers.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What three sequential stages define the classic Chemical Carcinogenesis model?
questions.explanation: Chemical carcinogenesis proceeds through initiation (irreversible DNA damage), promotion (cell proliferation), and progression (genomic instability and autonomy).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which cellular features characterize Malignant Anaplasia under microscopic examination?
options: Uniform cell size, preserved tissue polarity, and rare normal mitoses.
Cellular pleomorphism (variation in size and shape), hyperchromatic enlarged nuclei, high nuclear-to-cytoplasmic (N:C) ratio, and atypical mitoses.
Well-formed glandular tubules with abundant mucin secretion and low growth fraction.
Intact basement membranes separating epithelial nests from stroma.
questions.explanation: Anaplasia is marked by pleomorphism, high N:C ratio, hyperchromasia, abnormal mitoses, and loss of polarity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which circulating serum tumor marker is classically utilized for monitoring treatment response and recurrence in Ovarian Carcinoma?
questions.explanation: CA-125 is the primary serum marker used for monitoring ovarian carcinoma response and recurrence.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which core characteristic defines "Neoplasia" and separates it completely from normal hyperplastic tissue responses?
options: Coordinated, reversible growth driven by continuous hormonal stimulation.
Uncoordinated, autonomous growth that persists in the same excessive manner even after the initiating stimulus is withdrawn.
Multiclonal proliferation originating from multiple independent transformed parent cells.
Complete absence of any heritable genetic alterations within the proliferating cell population.
questions.explanation: Neoplasia is uncoordinated, autonomous, and clonal tissue growth that persists persistently after the inciting stimulus is removed.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which molecular changes facilitate tumor cell local invasion through the extracellular matrix (ECM)?
options: Upregulation of E-cadherin and suppression of cellular motility.
Loss of intercellular adhesion (e.g., reduced E-cadherin), degradation of ECM by proteases (e.g., matrix metalloproteinases), and acquisition of motility.
Complete synthesis of thick basement membranes surrounding individual cells.
Permanent arrest of all proteolytic enzyme transcription.
questions.explanation: Local invasion requires losing cell adhesion (decreased E-cadherin), releasing MMPs to digest ECM, and gaining cell motility.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which route of metastasis is traditionally favored by Carcinomas versus Sarcomas?
options: Carcinomas favor hematogenous spread; sarcomas favor direct cavity seeding.
Carcinomas favor lymphatic spread; sarcomas favor hematogenous spread.
Both carcinomas and sarcomas spread exclusively via lymphatic channels.
Both tumor types spread exclusively via perineural invasion.
questions.explanation: Carcinomas preferentially use lymphatics to reach regional nodes, while sarcomas favor hematogenous dissemination.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which serum biomarker serves as both a diagnostic aid and a monitoring tool for Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Yolk Sac Tumors?
questions.explanation: AFP is elevated in hepatocellular carcinoma and yolk sac tumors, aiding in diagnosis and disease monitoring.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which specialized staging system is universally applied to Lymphomas based on the number and location of involved lymph node regions relative to the diaphragm?
questions.explanation: Lymphomas are staged using the Ann Arbor system, mapping node involvement relative to the diaphragm.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which term designates a benign tumor arising from glandular epithelium, versus its malignant counterpart?
questions.explanation: Glandular tumors are named adenoma (benign) and adenocarcinoma (malignant) according to standard nomenclature.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is the metastatic cascade considered an intrinsically inefficient process for tumor cells?
options: Because tumor cells lack any ability to enter blood vessels.
Because only a small fraction of circulating tumor cells survive hemodynamic shear stress and immune attacks to establish a macroscopic metastatic deposit.
Because all metastatic cells instantly undergo spontaneous apoptosis inside lymph nodes.
Because host tissues actively inhibit angiogenesis everywhere in the body.
questions.explanation: Most shed tumor cells are destroyed by shear stress or immune clearance, making successful colonization a rare, inefficient event.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of progressive abdominal distension and early satiety. CT imaging shows a large, heterogeneous mass arising from the pancreas with areas of central necrosis and calcification. Fine‑needle aspiration cytology reveals malignant epithelial cells with glandular differentiation and mucin production. Which of the following histological features is most characteristic of the tumour type most likely responsible for this presentation?
options: Solid nests of spindle‑shaped cells with high mitotic activity
Sheets of pleomorphic cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm
Glandular structures lined by mucin‑producing epithelium with a desmoplastic stroma
Diffuse infiltration by small lymphoid cells forming lymphoid follicles
questions.explanation: The clinical scenario and imaging are classic for pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, which histologically shows glandular structures lined by malignant epithelial cells that produce mucin and are embedded in a desmoplastic stroma. The other options describe features of sarcoma, squamous cell carcinoma, and lymphoma, which are not typical for pancreatic adenocarcinoma.
questions.source: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma histology; basic surgical pathology principles
questions.topic: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma histology; basic surgical pathology principles
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 58‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of progressive abdominal distension and early satiety. CT imaging reveals a large, heterogeneous mass in the pancreatic head with central hypodensity and peripheral enhancement. Endoscopic ultrasound‑guided fine‑needle aspiration shows malignant epithelial cells forming glandular structures, but the cytology is inconclusive for differentiation. Which histopathological feature, if identified on a surgical resection specimen, would most strongly support the diagnosis of pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma over a neuroendocrine tumour?
options: Presence of desmoplastic stromal reaction with abundant collagen deposition
Identification of chromogranin A‑positive cells in nests
Detection of GATA‑3 nuclear staining in tumour cells
questions.explanation: Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma is characterised by a pronounced desmoplastic stroma with dense collagen deposition. Neuroendocrine tumours typically express chromogranin A and lack a desmoplastic reaction. GATA‑3 is a marker for breast and urothelial tumours, not pancreatic adenocarcinoma. Signet‑ring cells are associated with mucinous adenocarcinomas of other sites. Thus, a desmoplastic stromal reaction best distinguishes ductal adenocarcinoma.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the lecture's final summary, what is the golden rule regarding biopsy selection and communication with the pathologist?
options: Choose biopsy type based on size, site, and suspected diagnosis (no one-size-fits-all approach), and communicate directly with the pathologist to prevent delays and ensure appropriate testing
Always perform a shave biopsy for every skin lesion and avoid calling the lab
Always put every specimen in normal saline first
Slice all tumors in half before sending them to pathology
questions.explanation: Tailoring the biopsy modality to the clinical lesion and maintaining direct surgeon-pathologist communication maximizes diagnostic accuracy and patient safety.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Can molecular studies (DNA/RNA mutation analysis) be performed on routine Formalin-Fixed Paraffin-Embedded (FFPE) tissue blocks?
options: No, molecular studies are strictly impossible on FFPE blocks
Yes — while fresh tissue is optimal, FFPE blocks are adequate for routine molecular studies
Only if fixed in normal saline
Only if frozen in liquid nitrogen
questions.explanation: Modern PCR and Next-Generation Sequencing (NGS) protocols routinely extract DNA/RNA from well-fixed FFPE blocks.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: For optimal Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and breast hormone receptor (ER/PR/HER2) assessment, within what timeframe post-excision should tissue ideally be placed in 10% NBF?
options: Within ≤ 1 hour post-excision (cold ischemia time < 1 hour)
After 12 hours on the surgical bench
Timing does not affect receptor status
questions.explanation: Prolonged cold ischemia (>1 hour) degrades labile receptor proteins (especially ER/PR/HER2), causing false-negative predictive biomarker results.

questions.stem: How does the pathologist examine the external surface and cut surfaces during Gross Examination?
options: By naked eye inspection, measuring 3D dimensions, describing macroscopic appearance, and sectioning according to orientation
questions.explanation: Thorough grossing selects the most representative blocks (tumor, margins, lymph nodes) for microscopic embedding.

questions.stem: How long does an intra-operative Frozen Section consultation typically take to report back to the surgeon?
questions.explanation: Frozen section provides rapid intra-operative pathologic feedback within 15–30 minutes while the patient remains under anesthesia.

questions.stem: How many unique patient identifiers are mandatory on every surgical specimen label?
options: At least ONE (e.g., first name only)
At least TWO patient identifiers (e.g., Patient full name as per ID with no abbreviations + Date of birth / Hospital ID)
Zero identifiers if the surgeon signs the form
questions.explanation: Using at least two unique identifiers (full name + DOB/hospital MRN) eliminates misidentification between patients with similar names.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla

questions.stem: How MUST a tissue specimen for Frozen Section be transported to the pathology laboratory?
options: NEVER fix in formalin — send FRESH, immediately on ice or dry, with prior notification to the lab
questions.explanation: Formalin fixes tissue proteins and prevents freezing in the cryostat; frozen section specimens must arrive fresh and unfixed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How should Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) samples be handled immediately after collection?
options: Prepared as air-dried or wet-fixed smears (plus a cell block if bloody/fluid-rich)
questions.explanation: Air-dried smears are stained with Giemsa/Diff-Quik while alcohol wet-fixed smears are stained with Papanicolaou stain.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: If a lymph node biopsy is suspected to be a lymphoma requiring Flow Cytometry, how must the specimen be submitted?
options: Must be sent FRESH (unfixed) immediately to the laboratory
questions.explanation: Flow cytometry requires viable, intact cell suspensions to immunophenotype surface markers; formalin fixation cross-links proteins and kills cells.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: If a surgical specimen requires Microbiology Culture (e.g., suspected tuberculous lymphadenitis or abscess), how must it be submitted?
options: Must be sent FRESH in a sterile container without fixative
questions.explanation: Formalin is bactericidal and destroys microorganisms, rendering culture impossible.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the classic clinical indications for an Excisional Biopsy?
options: Small skin lesions, enlarged lymph nodes, and small soft tissue masses
questions.explanation: When a lesion is small enough to be completely removed with clear margins safely, excisional biopsy achieves both diagnosis and cure.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the classic organ indications and potential complications/limitations of Core Needle Biopsy (CNB)?
options: Indications: Breast, prostate, liver, kidney, lung, bone; Limitations: Sampling error and hematoma risk
Indications: Cornea and retina; Limitations: Cataract
Indications: Epidermal warts only; Limitations: Keloid
questions.explanation: CNB is the standard pre-operative biopsy for breast, prostate, liver, and renal masses, requiring immediate 10% NBF fixation.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the four 'Golden Rules for Orientation' of surgical specimens?
options: 1. Agree on a suture convention with pathology and apply consistently; 2. Attach orientation note & communicate verbally; 3. Never re-orient after excision (orient in situ if possible); 4. Document orientation diagram in operative note
1. Cut specimen first; 2. Guess orientation after fixation; 3. Label lid only; 4. Use non-waterproof ink
1. Place in saline; 2. Freeze before inking; 3. Omit clinical history; 4. Send next month
1. Use one jar for all tumors; 2. Never draw diagrams; 3. Ignore close margins; 4. Skip sutures
questions.explanation: Once an irregular soft-tissue or breast specimen is removed from the body, it loses its anatomical landmarks and cannot be reliably oriented retrospectively.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the histological consequences of 'Fixation Artefact' (delayed or inadequate fixation)?
options: Cell swelling, shrinkage, and poor staining quality
questions.explanation: Inadequate fixation causes uneven dye uptake and structural collapse during paraffin processing.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the six main sections (A–F) of a complete Pathology Request Form?
options: A. Patient Demographics; B. Clinical Information; C. Specimen Details; D. Investigations Required; E. Surgeon's Details; F. Special Instructions
A. Anesthesia chart; B. Nursing notes; C. Fluid balance; D. Pharmacy bill; E. Diet sheet; F. Discharge summary
Only Specimen Weight and Fixative Volume
questions.explanation: A complete request form bridges the clinical gap between surgeon and pathologist.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla

questions.stem: What are the three primary intra-operative indications for a Frozen Section (FS) biopsy?
options: Margin assessment, lymph node status (e.g., sentinel node), and distinguishing benign vs. malignant lesions intra-operatively
Routine diagnosis of fatty lipomas, bone tumors, and dry necrotic eschars
Electron microscopy, microbiology culture, and flow cytometry
questions.explanation: Frozen section is only indicated when the immediate intra-operative result will directly alter the surgical procedure being performed.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the two mandatory requirements for safe SPECIMEN TRANSPORTATION to the pathology laboratory?
options: 1. Secure, leak-proof lid; 2. Proper biohazard precaution (secondary biohazard bag/carrier)
1. Open container lid; 2. Transport in surgeon's pocket
1. Plastic bag without any rigid container; 2. Delayed overnight storage at room temperature
1. Wrapping in dry paper towels; 2. Leaving at reception desk
questions.explanation: Formalin is toxic/carcinogenic and fresh tissues carry infectious risk; rigid containers with tight lids inside sealed biohazard bags are mandatory.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What causes 'Crush Artefact', and how does it affect microscopic diagnosis?
options: Leaving tissue in formalin for 24 hours
Squeezing or grasping delicate tissue tightly with forceps or clamps, causing severe nuclear smearing and artificial distortion
Using waterproof ink on the container
Placing a short suture at the superior pole
questions.explanation: Forceps crush shears fragile nuclei (especially in small biopsies and lymphoid/neuroendocrine tumors), obscuring cellular detail.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What causes 'Drying Artefact', and what is its histological consequence?
options: Leaving tissue exposed on a dry surgical tray or dry gauze, causing severe cellular shrinkage and distortion
questions.explanation: Evaporation of cellular water causes pyknotic, hyperchromatic, distorted cells that cannot be reliably evaluated.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) collect, and what are its classic clinical indications?
options: Large bone cylinders; indicated for osteosarcoma
Samples of cells and fluid using a very small needle; indicated for thyroid nodules, lymph nodes, salivary glands, and superficial soft tissue masses
Full-thickness skin cores; indicated for psoriasis
Whole organ resections; indicated for staging
questions.explanation: FNA is a rapid, minimally invasive outpatient cytological sampling technique ideal for thyroid, salivary, and nodal lesions.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What happens if a fresh, unfixed surgical specimen experiences a transport delay of > 30 minutes without refrigeration or fixation?
options: Risk of tissue autolysis (enzymatic self-digestion) and drying artefact
questions.explanation: Delayed immersion in formalin initiates lysosomal autolysis and bacterial overgrowth, permanently ruining cellular morphology.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What happens if an unfixed specimen is sent in a dry container taking > 30 minutes to reach the lab?
options: Autolysis and drying artefact degrade cellular morphology
questions.explanation: Rapid transport (<30 min) or immediate 10% NBF immersion is mandatory to preserve tissue integrity.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What happens if an UNLABELED surgical specimen arrives at the pathology department?
options: The pathologist guesses the patient's name
The specimen is REJECTED (cannot be processed safely), potentially requiring a repeat invasive procedure and causing severe patient harm
It is automatically reported as benign
It is discarded without notifying the surgeon
questions.explanation: Processing an unlabeled specimen risks issuing a cancer diagnosis to the wrong patient; strict laboratory safety mandates rejection/quarantine.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a 'Tissue Artefact' in diagnostic pathology?
options: An artificial distortion of tissue induced during the biopsy procedure, surgical handling, or laboratory processing
questions.explanation: Artefacts mimic or obscure true pathology (e.g., crush artefact mimicking small cell carcinoma) and can render a biopsy uninterpretable.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a major cause of false-negative or missed diagnoses directly related to biopsy technique?
options: Sampling error (failing to obtain a sample that truly represents the lesion)
Submitting a clinical history on the request form
Labeling the container with two identifiers
questions.explanation: Sampling necrotic centers or adjacent reactive tissue instead of viable diagnostic lesion leads to false-negative pathology reports.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla

questions.stem: What is a Punch Biopsy, and what are its primary dermatological indications?
options: A superficial horizontal slice; used for seborrheic keratosis
A cylindrical full-thickness skin sample (2–8 mm); indicated for inflammatory dermatoses and melanocytic lesions
A hollow needle biopsy of the liver
questions.explanation: A 2–8 mm circular punch blade obtains epidermis, dermis, and subcutis in a single full-thickness cylinder.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is an Excisional Biopsy, and how should the surgeon handle the specimen before sending it to the lab?
options: Partial removal; cut it into multiple slices in theatre
Complete removal of the entire lesion (both diagnostic and therapeutic); DO NOT section before sending to the lab, and document orientation with sutures
Superficial shave biopsy; leave on a dry tray for 2 hours
Needle aspiration; place in normal saline
questions.explanation: Never bivalve or slice an excisional specimen in the OR, as this destroys margin integrity and prevents accurate inking by the pathologist.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is an Incisional Biopsy, and what is its clinical goal?
options: Complete removal of a small lesion; both diagnostic and curative
Partial removal of a lesion; goal is diagnosis ONLY (NOT curative)
Superficial horizontal shave of the epidermis
questions.explanation: Incisional biopsy is reserved for large tumors or mucosal/soft-tissue masses where complete excision requires definitive pre-operative histological diagnosis.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is considered the 'cornerstone of diagnosis' during microscopic analysis of a surgical specimen?
options: Tissue architecture, disease pattern, and cellular/nuclear morphology
questions.explanation: Evaluation of cellular and nuclear morphology alongside architectural arrangement remains the definitive foundation of histopathology.

questions.stem: What is the approximate tissue penetration rate of 10% Neutral Buffered Formalin?
questions.explanation: Because formalin penetrates slowly (~1 mm/hr), large solid organs must be sliced (after inking) to allow fixative access to deep tumors.

questions.stem: What is the consequence of 'Illegible handwriting' on a Pathology Request Form?
options: Transcription errors, reporting delays, and risk of assigning a report to the wrong patient
None, as handwritten forms are not read
questions.explanation: Printed electronic orders or clear block capital letters prevent misreading of patient names, sites, and clinical notes.
questions.source: Principles of Diagnostic & Surgical Pathology — Lecture 1, Dr. Alla S. Addalla

questions.stem: What is the consequence of omitting clinical history on the Pathology Request Form?
options: Non-specific reporting and failure to consider important differential diagnoses
questions.explanation: Clinical context transforms a descriptive histological observation into an actionable specific diagnosis.

questions.stem: What is the consequence of providing 'Inadequate fixation details' on the Pathology Request Form?
options: Immunohistochemistry (IHC) and molecular tests may fail or yield invalid results
questions.explanation: Different fixatives (e.g., Bouin's or alcohol vs. 10% NBF) alter antigen retrieval protocols and nucleic acid integrity.

questions.stem: What is the consequence of writing the 'Wrong site or no laterality' (e.g., omitting Left vs. Right breast) on the label or request form?
options: Minor delay with no clinical impact
Specimens mixed up, re-excision performed at the wrong anatomical site, and severe medicolegal consequences
questions.explanation: Never-event surgical errors (operating on the wrong side) frequently trace back to omitted or inaccurate laterality on pathology forms.

questions.stem: What is the correct 5-step sequence for handling surgical specimens in the operating theatre?
options: 1. Remove Cleanly → 2. Orient & Ink → 3. Measure → 4. Fix Promptly → 5. Label Correctly
1. Cut into pieces → 2. Leave on dry tray → 3. Put in saline → 4. Label lid → 5. Send next week
1. Fix in formalin → 2. Send for frozen section → 3. Crush with forceps → 4. Wash ink off
1. Label lid → 2. Place in plastic bag without pot → 3. Add tap water
questions.explanation: Following this exact workflow preserves tissue morphology, margin orientation, and patient identity.

questions.stem: What is the expected turnaround time for small biopsies versus large or complex surgical resection specimens?
options: Small biopsies: 1–3 working days; Large/complex specimens: 5–10 working days or longer
Small biopsies: 10–14 days; Large specimens: 15 minutes
Large specimens are always reported faster than small biopsies
questions.explanation: Large resections require overnight fixation, extensive grossing, multiple tissue blocks, and decalcification/special stains if needed.

questions.stem: What is the golden technical rule when performing an Incisional Biopsy regarding tissue selection?
options: Sample exclusively from the central necrotic core
Include the interface of normal and abnormal tissue, and AVOID central necrotic areas (submit viable peripheral tissue)
Crush the tissue with toothed forceps before fixation
Mix samples from multiple sites into a single formalin pot
questions.explanation: Central tumor necrosis yields non-diagnostic debris; the viable periphery and normal-tumor transition zone show active invasion.

Preventing crush artefact during forceps handling
Determining the exact time of specimen collection
questions.explanation: Molecular profiling detects actionable mutations (e.g., BRAF, EGFR, KRAS) that direct targeted oncological therapies.

FNA cannot be used on thyroid nodules

All specimens are automatically treated as frozen sections
questions.explanation: Flagging urgent/cancer-suspect cases prioritizes rapid tissue processing and expedited pathologist sign-out.

questions.stem: What is the primary basis of 'Morphological Diagnosis' in diagnostic surgical pathology?

questions.explanation: Morphological diagnosis combines naked-eye gross inspection with microscopic evaluation of architecture and cytomorphology.

All margins painted with water-soluble pen
Ink is applied only after paraffin embedding

Orient, measure, and immerse it promptly in 10% NBF (unless fresh tissue is needed for frozen section, flow cytometry, or culture)
Wash it vigorously with tap water for 20 minutes
Squeeze it with hemostats to remove blood

Submitted in separate, individually labeled containers specifying each exact anatomical site
Wrapped together in a single gauze sponge

Using a water-soluble pencil that washes off in formalin
Only after the pathologist asks for it

On the outside of the transport bag only

In the pathology laboratory after gross sectioning

questions.stem: How must a surgical tissue specimen intended for intraoperative Frozen Section (FS) consultation be handled and transported to the laboratory?

Placed in 0.9% Normal Saline for 1 hour
Sent completely fresh immediately on ice or dry (NEVER fixed in formalin)

Timing does not affect receptor preservation

Automatic execution of molecular DNA sequencing

questions.stem: What is the primary diagnostic limitation of Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) compared to Core Needle Biopsy (CNB)?

FNA provides no tissue architecture, making it impossible to distinguish in-situ from invasive carcinoma
FNA cannot aspirate fluid from cystic neck masses
FNA requires routine general anesthesia in an operating suite

Black = Superior; Blue = Inferior; Yellow = Anterior; Green = Posterior

questions.stem: Why is a shave biopsy strictly contraindicated when evaluating a patient for suspected cutaneous malignant melanoma?
