White = Loose tissue with venous occlusion; Red = Solid organs with single arterial supply
White = Organs affected exclusively by septic emboli; Red = Organs affected by sterile fat emboli
White = CNS tissue; Red = Cardiac muscle only
questions.explanation: White (anemic) infarcts occur following arterial occlusion in solid organs with single end-arterial blood supplies (e.g., heart, spleen, kidney), where tissue density limits hemorrhage. Red (hemorrhagic) infarcts occur in loose tissues (lung), organs with dual blood supply (lung, small intestine), sites of venous occlusion (testicular torsion, bowel strangulation), or tissue subjected to arterial reperfusion.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What anatomical site accounts for more than 95% of all Pulmonary Thromboemboli (PE)?
options: Superficial veins of the upper arm (cephalic and basilic veins)
Deep veins of the lower extremities (femoral, popliteal, and iliac veins)
questions.explanation: Over 95% of pulmonary thromboemboli originate from deep vein thrombosis (DVT) involving the proximal deep veins of the lower limbs above the knee—specifically the femoral, popliteal, and iliac veins.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are "Heart Failure Cells" in the context of chronic passive pulmonary congestion?
options: Hypertrophied myocardial cells circulating in the pulmonary venules
Hemosiderin-laden alveolar macrophages formed after phagocytosing extravasated red blood cells
Apoptotic type II pneumocytes shed into the alveolar spaces
Neutrophils forming extracellular traps inside pulmonary capillaries
questions.explanation: Chronic pulmonary congestion (usually from left heart failure or mitral stenosis) engorges septal capillaries and leads to microhemorrhages into alveoli. Alveolar macrophages phagocytose the extravasated erythrocytes and break down hemoglobin into golden-brown hemosiderin, becoming "heart failure cells."
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are "Lines of Zahn," and in which type of thrombus are they characteristically observed?
options: Concentric bacterial rings seen in postmortem clots
Alternating pale layers (platelets and fibrin) and dark layers (erythrocytes) seen in arterial ("white") thrombi formed in flowing blood
Deposits of calcium soaps in fat necrosis
Fibrinoid deposits within necrotic capillary walls
questions.explanation: Lines of Zahn are alternating pale bands of aggregated platelets and fibrin interleaved with darker bands of red blood cells. They represent laminations produced as blood flows past a forming clot and are characteristic of arterial ("white") thrombi and cardiac mural thrombi, proving the clot formed during life.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the five possible clinical and pathological fates of a newly formed thrombus?
options: Propagation, Embolization, Dissolution, Organization, and Recanalization
Hyperemia, Congestion, Transudation, Exudation, and Calcification
Pyknosis, Karyorrhexis, Karyolysis, Suppuration, and Gangrene
Saponification, Caseation, Liquefaction, Fibrinoid decay, and Erosion
questions.explanation: A thrombus can undergo five potential fates: (1) Propagation (enlarging to occlude the vessel), (2) Embolization (dislodging to travel elsewhere), (3) Dissolution (cleared by rapid fibrinolysis), (4) Organization (ingrowth of endothelial cells, smooth muscle, and fibroblasts), and (5) Recanalization (formation of new capillary channels restoring partial flow).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What estimated minimum volume of intravenous air is required to produce a life-threatening "gas lock" in the right ventricular outflow tract?
questions.explanation: While tiny air bubbles introduced during IV therapy are absorbed harmlessly, approximately 100 mL or more of air introduced rapidly into the venous system (e.g., via neck/chest trauma, central line insertion/removal, or laparoscopic insufflation) can create a fatal "gas lock" obstructing right ventricular outflow.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What features characterize the Nonprogressive (Compensated) stage of Shock?
options: Compensatory neurohormonal reflex mechanisms (tachycardia, peripheral vasoconstriction, renal fluid retention) maintain vital organ perfusion
Complete breakdown of blood pressure leading to severe metabolic acidosis
Widespread multi-organ dysfunction syndrome and refractory hypotension
Immediate resolution of shock without any cardiovascular response
questions.explanation: In Stage 1 (Nonprogressive/Compensated Shock), neurohormonal reflexes—including baroreceptor activation, sympathetic tachycardia, peripheral cutaneous/visceral vasoconstriction, and renal fluid conservation via RAAS/ADH—maintain blood pressure and blood flow to critical organs (brain and heart). Identifying shock at this stage before overt hypotension develops is essential.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a "Saddle Embolus," and what is its primary acute clinical outcome?
options: A tiny embolus in a renal arteriole causing microscopic hematuria
A large embolus straddling the main pulmonary artery bifurcation, often causing sudden death
A fat globule trapped in a cerebral capillary causing focal seizures
A air bubble lodged in the coronary artery
questions.explanation: A saddle embolus is a massive thromboembolus that lodges at the bifurcation of the main pulmonary artery trunk, straddling both right and left pulmonary arteries. It acutely blocks pulmonary blood flow, precipitating acute right heart failure (cor pulmonale) or sudden cardiac arrest.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the "rule of thumb" regarding acute blood loss and the development of hemorrhagic shock?
options: Acute loss of more than ~5% of blood volume causes immediate cardiac arrest
Acute loss of more than ~20% of blood volume risks hemorrhagic shock
Patients easily tolerate acute loss of 50% blood volume without hemodynamic changes
Shock occurs only when blood loss is chronic over several months
questions.explanation: Volume lost is the single most important determinant of the clinical impact of hemorrhage. As a clinical rule of thumb, acute loss of more than approximately 20% of total blood volume risks precipitating hemorrhagic shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental pathophysiological mechanism that distinguishes Active Hyperemia from Passive Congestion?
options: Hyperemia is a passive process caused by impaired arterial inflow; Congestion is an active process caused by dilated veins
Hyperemia is an active process driven by arteriolar/capillary dilation (increased blood inflow); Congestion is a passive process driven by impaired venous outflow
Hyperemia occurs exclusively in response to right heart failure; Congestion occurs only during skeletal muscle exercise
Hyperemia produces cool cyanotic tissue; Congestion produces warm erythematous tissue
questions.explanation: Hyperemia is an active process resulting from arteriolar dilation that increases blood inflow, causing tissue to become redder and warmer (e.g., exercise, inflammation). Congestion is a passive process resulting from impaired venous drainage, causing blood backup that turns tissue blue-red (cyanotic) and cooler (e.g., heart failure, venous obstruction).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What macroscopic and microscopic features define the classic "Nutmeg Liver" in chronic passive hepatic congestion?
options: Uniform pale yellow discoloration across all lobules due to glycogen overload
Centrilobular congestion, microhemorrhage, and necrosis paired with periportal (Zone 1) fatty change, creating a red-brown mottled cut surface
Diffuse fibrous portal tract replacement with total central vein preservation
Multiple fluid-filled abscesses lined by granulating tissue
questions.explanation: Chronic passive hepatic congestion (typically from right heart failure) causes blood to pool in central veins, producing centrilobular congestion, microhemorrhage, and necrosis (dark red areas). Surrounding periportal hepatocytes undergo hypoxia-induced fatty change (yellowish areas), yielding a mottled cut surface resembling a nutmeg kernel. Long-standing cases progress to "cardiac sclerosis."
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What three pathological factors constitute Virchow's Triad in thrombosis?
options: Endothelial injury, abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and hypercoagulability
Arterial vasospasm, venous dilation, and lymphatic blockage
questions.explanation: Virchow's triad outlines the primary predisposing factors for pathological thrombosis: (1) Endothelial injury (the most critical factor for arterial and cardiac thrombi), (2) Abnormal blood flow (stasis or turbulence), and (3) Hypercoagulability (inherited or acquired). Surgical trauma classically triggers all three factors simultaneously.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What type of cutaneous or mucosal hemorrhage is defined as pinpoint lesions measuring 1 to 2 mm, typically indicating low platelet count or platelet dysfunction?
questions.explanation: Petechiae are pinpoint hemorrhages measuring 1–2 mm, typically caused by severe thrombocytopenia or defective platelet function. Purpura refers to slightly larger lesions (>3 mm), ecchymoses are larger subcutaneous bruises (1–2 cm), and a hematoma is a confined mass of blood within a tissue space.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which set of physiological mechanisms accounts for the four primary causes of clinical Edema?
options: Increased hydrostatic pressure, decreased plasma oncotic pressure, lymphatic obstruction, and sodium/water retention
Decreased hydrostatic pressure, increased oncotic pressure, arteriolar spasm, and hypokalemia
Primary capillary calcification, acute thrombocytosis, hypercalcemia, and metabolic alkalosis
Increased systemic vascular resistance, decreased ADH secretion, hyperalbuminemia, and diuresis
questions.explanation: Edema occurs whenever capillary filtration exceeds reabsorption and lymphatic clearance. The four primary pathophysiological mechanisms are: (1) Increased hydrostatic pressure (e.g., heart failure, DVT), (2) Decreased plasma oncotic pressure (e.g., liver failure, nephrotic syndrome), (3) Lymphatic obstruction (e.g., lymph node dissection, tumor), and (4) Sodium and water retention (e.g., renal failure, RAAS activation).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A person lacks capacity if their mind is impaired or disturbed. Which of the following is explicitly listed in the lecture as a clinical cause of impaired capacity?
options: Mild fatigue after a normal working day
Mental health conditions, dementia, severe learning disabilities, brain damage (e.g., stroke/injury), or intoxication by alcohol or drugs
Normal physiological aging without cognitive decline
questions.explanation: Impairment of capacity results from conditions affecting mental function, including mental health disorders, dementia, severe learning disabilities, brain damage (stroke/trauma), and acute intoxication from alcohol or drugs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A person's capacity to consent can fluctuate over time. Which transient physiological or psychological states can temporarily impair capacity?
options: Normal circadian rhythm and healthy diet
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and fluid; it can be temporarily compromised by acute shock, severe panic, extreme fatigue, or sedating/psychoactive medications.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the lecture guidelines, during which of the following clinical encounters is taking consent required?
options: Major surgical operations under general anesthesia only
History taking, physical examination, performing investigations, procedures, surgery, anesthesia, high-risk medications, treatment, and research
High-risk medication administration and clinical research exclusively
questions.explanation: Consent is needed across every patient encounter, including history taking, physical examination, diagnostic investigations, clinical procedures, surgical interventions, general anesthesia, high-risk medications, treatment, and research.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, how is medical consent formally defined?
options: A financial agreement binding the patient to hospital fees
To give permission or agreement to receive any type of medical treatment, test, examination, or communication
A legal waiver transferring all surgical liability from the physician to the patient
An authorization given exclusively by a court judge prior to emergency intervention
questions.explanation: Consent is defined as giving permission or agreement to receive any type of medical treatment, test, examination, or communication.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to the lecture, obtaining consent is fundamentally essential for which key ethical, professional, and legal principle?
options: Respect for patient autonomy and self-determination
Complete immunity from hospital administrative audits
Maximizing surgical patient throughput per day
questions.explanation: Obtaining consent is a fundamental principle of medical law and ethics, serving as an essential demonstration of respect for patient autonomy and self-determination.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: During the communication process of obtaining informed consent, which of the following details must be clearly explained to the patient?
options: Only the anticipated benefits of the surgical procedure
Why treatment is needed, risks/complications, benefits, expected outcomes, alternative treatments (with their risks/benefits/outcomes), and what happens if treatment is refused
The cost of surgical instruments and hospital operating fees
Only the risks associated with refusing the proposed procedure
questions.explanation: Full disclosure requires explaining why treatment is needed, its risks and complications, benefits, expected outcomes, alternative treatments (including their risks, benefits, and outcomes), and the consequences of non-treatment or refusal.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is "Capacity" defined in the context of medical consent?
options: The physical ability of an organ system to withstand surgical stress
The ability to understand and use information to make a decision and communicate any decision made
Being at least 21 years of age with full legal status
The physiological respiratory volume during general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Capacity is defined as the functional ability to understand and use relevant information to make a healthcare decision and to communicate that decision.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: If an immediate additional emergency procedure becomes necessary during an ongoing surgical operation, what is the consent rule stated in the lecture?
options: The surgeon must pause surgery and awaken the patient to obtain verbal consent
Consent is not needed for immediate additional emergency procedures during an operation
Surgery must be terminated immediately and rescheduled
The procedure can only proceed if a court order is obtained in theatre
questions.explanation: Consent is not required if other immediate additional emergency procedures become necessary during the course of an ongoing operation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In which clinical scenario is obtaining consent explicitly NOT required according to the lecture guidelines?
options: Routine elective herniorrhaphy in a competent adult
Emergency treatment needed to save life in an unconscious patient
questions.explanation: Consent is not needed when emergency treatment is required immediately to save life in an unconscious patient where delay would cause harm.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Medical consent is NOT required for treating a patient with a severe mental health condition (such as schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or dementia) under which specific condition?
options: The patient is over 65 years old
The patient lacks the capacity to consent
The patient is admitted to a private hospital ward
The patient has a history of essential hypertension
questions.explanation: Consent is not needed for patients with severe mental health conditions (e.g., schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, dementia) specifically when the patient lacks the decision-making capacity to consent.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Regarding the timeline of consent, when does a patient retain the legal and ethical right to withdraw their consent?
options: Only within 24 hours of signing the written consent form
At any time before the start of the intervention or treatment
Only after consulting a hospital legal representative
Patients cannot withdraw consent once it has been documented in the chart
questions.explanation: A patient retains the right to withdraw their consent at any point prior to the commencement of the intervention or treatment.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Under what circumstances can life support treatment be stopped according to the lecture protocol?
options: Unilaterally by the attending doctor without consulting family
When there is agreement that continuing treatment is not in the person's best interest, after discussion with relatives and friends
Automatically after 72 hours in all intensive care cases
Only if the patient leaves a written financial bequest to the hospital
questions.explanation: Life support can be stopped if there is consensus that continuing treatment is not in the patient's best interest, established through discussions with relatives and friends (with court referral if agreement fails).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the two explicit types of consent categorized in the lecture material?
questions.explanation: The lecture explicitly categorizes consent into two types: Verbal consent and Written consent.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What constitutes an "Informed Consent" as defined in the presentation?
options: A signed form obtained quickly without detailed discussion to save clinic time
Obtaining consent after full explanation and education to the patient about treatment, intervention, or research
Verbal agreement obtained while the patient is under sedating premedication
A unilateral decision made by the attending physician in the patient's best interest
questions.explanation: Informed consent is defined as obtaining permission after full explanation and education provided to the patient regarding the treatment, intervention, or research project.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the "Voluntary" element of an informed consent specifically mandate?
options: The patient pays for all medical procedures out of pocket
The patient is not under pressure or coercion to give consent
The patient agrees to participate in clinical research without financial compensation
The patient undergoes surgery on a non-emergency weekend schedule
questions.explanation: Voluntariness means the patient gives consent freely and is not under external pressure or coercion from family, staff, or circumstances.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What legal action can be taken if a person with parental responsibility refuses medical treatment for a child that may lead to death or severe permanent injury?
options: The child must be discharged without treatment immediately
The refusal decision can be overruled by the court
The attending physician is held criminally liable if they report the case
questions.explanation: If a parent/guardian refuses treatment for a child that could lead to death or severe permanent injury, the court has the authority to overrule that refusal to protect the child.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When should patient capacity be assessed, and who is authorized to conduct the assessment?
options: At hospital admission by an administrative clerk
At the time consent is required, conducted by an appropriately trained and experienced health professional who is either recommending or involved in carrying out the treatment
After completion of the surgical procedure by a recovery room nurse
Exclusively by a court-appointed judge prior to any clinical encounter
questions.explanation: Capacity must be assessed at the exact time consent is required by an appropriately trained healthcare professional who is recommending or executing the procedure.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which four core elements must be observed for an informed consent to be considered valid?
options: Age, Financial status, Legal representation, and Notarization
Comprehension, Voluntariness, Informed state, and Capacity
Written signature, Witness presence, Hospital approval, and Pre-payment
Physician authority, Family approval, Emergency status, and Documentation
questions.explanation: For a consent to be valid, four essential elements must be observed: Comprehension (patient understands clearly), Voluntariness (free of pressure), Informed state (knows risks, benefits, and alternatives), and Capacity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following is explicitly listed as a major issue of concern or barrier regarding informed consent in clinical practice?
options: Lack of patient comprehension, language barriers, cultural differences, time pressures, changing medical circumstances, incomplete disclosure, and inadequate documentation
Excessive time available for doctor-patient discussion
Universal health literacy among all surgical patients
questions.explanation: Major challenges in obtaining valid informed consent include lack of patient comprehension, language barriers, cultural differences, severe time pressures, fluid medical circumstances, incomplete disclosure, and inadequate documentation.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Who holds the legal authority to give medical consent for children and young people up to the age of 16 to 18 years?
options: Any attending healthcare worker in the hospital
Anyone with parental responsibility (child, mother, appointed guardian, or court)
The child alone regardless of parental involvement
questions.explanation: Consent for children up to 16–18 years should be given by anyone possessing parental responsibility, which includes the child, mother, appointed legal guardian, or the court.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: At what stage of a patient encounter is consent required?
options: Exclusively prior to general anesthesia and skin incisions.
In any clinical encounter, including history taking, physical examination, investigations, and procedures.
Only when prescribing high-risk experimental medications.
questions.explanation: Consent is required across all clinical interactions, from basic history taking and physical examination to diagnostic tests and surgical interventions.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Can a person's capacity to consent fluctuate or change over time?
options: No, capacity is a permanent legal attribute established at birth.
Yes, capacity can change; individuals may manage simple decisions but lack capacity for complex long-term treatments, or have temporary impairments due to shock, panic, or psychosis.
Capacity only changes if confirmed by a supreme court judge.
Once impaired, capacity can never be recovered.
questions.explanation: Capacity is decision-specific and time-dependent; it can fluctuate due to medical states, psychiatric episodes, shock, or medications.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: During the "Setting up" (S) step of SPIKES, what environmental factor is most critical?
options: Conducting the conversation in a busy, active hallway for transparency.
Ensuring privacy, arranging comfortable seating at eye-level, eliminating interruptions (phones, pagers, staff), and allowing support persons if desired.
Standing directly over the patient's bed to project clinical authority.
Turning off all room lights to calm the patient.
questions.explanation: Proper setting requires privacy, unhurried time, eye-level positioning, absence of interruptions, and welcoming chosen family or support staff.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How do cultural differences influence patients' preferences when receiving bad news or discussing terminal diagnoses?
options: All cultures globally share identical preferences for direct disclosure.
Cultural and spiritual beliefs vary significantly; for instance, some cultures or immigrant groups may believe discussing death brings it closer, requiring tailored, sensitive communication.
Cultural background has zero impact on medical communication.
Physicians should ignore cultural nuances to maintain standard hospital protocols.
questions.explanation: Studies demonstrate wide cultural variations in preferences for disclosure and end-of-life decision-making, necessitating cultural sensitivity from clinicians.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How does Islamic medical ethics view the sanctity of human life?
options: Life is valued only if the individual possesses economic utility.
Life is sacred, and Islam places profound emphasis on preserving, protecting, and respecting life in all its stages.
Preservation of life is secondary to institutional convenience.
Medical intervention is prohibited when illness strikes.
questions.explanation: Islamic medical ethics stresses the sanctity of human life, preservation of health, benevolence (Ihsan), and avoiding harm ("La darar wa la dirar").
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is "Bad News" formally defined in a clinical context?
options: Any diagnostic test result that takes longer than 48 hours to process.
Any information which adversely and seriously affects an individual's view of their future, or creates feelings of no hope or a threat to mental/physical well-being.
A minor surgical complication that resolves spontaneously.
Any hospital administrative policy change affecting visiting hours.
questions.explanation: Bad news is defined as any information that severely and adversely alters a person's outlook on their future or threatens their well-being.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is medical consent formally defined?
options: A financial contract binding the patient to hospital fees.
Permission or agreement given by a person to receive any type of medical treatment, test, examination, or communication.
A legal waiver transferring all medical liability from the doctor to the patient.
A verbal agreement required only before major abdominal surgery.
questions.explanation: Consent is permission or agreement given for any medical examination, investigation, treatment, or procedure.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is patient "Capacity" defined in the context of medical consent?
options: The legal status of being over 18 years of age.
The ability of an individual to understand, retain, and use information to make a healthcare decision and communicate that decision.
The physical stamina required to withstand general anesthesia.
The financial capability to pay for private medical treatment.
questions.explanation: Capacity refers to a person's functional mental ability to process information, weigh options, make a decision, and communicate it at the time consent is needed.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How should a clinician respond to patient "Emotions" (E) such as shock, crying, or silence according to the SPIKES model?
options: Immediately change the subject to lighten the mood.
Identify the emotion, connect with empathy (e.g., "I can see how upsetting this is to you"), allow silence, and offer realistic hope.
Tell the patient not to cry because everything will definitely be cured.
Leave the room immediately to give them privacy.
questions.explanation: Emotional responses require empathetic acknowledgment, validating statements, tolerance of silence, and compassionate support.
questions.topic: Breaking bad news: responding to emotions
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Under which of the following circumstances is consent NOT legally required?
options: Elective cosmetic plastic surgery in a fully conscious adult.
Emergency treatment required immediately to save a life or in unconscious patients where delay would cause permanent harm.
Outpatient physical therapy for chronic back pain.
Diagnostic blood tests during a routine annual check-up.
questions.explanation: Emergency life-saving treatment in unconscious patients or immediate intraoperative life-saving procedures do not require prior formal consent.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What are the essential core elements required for a valid informed consent?
options: Written signature, notary verification, and witness approval.
Comprehension, Voluntariness, Being Informed, and Capacity.
Financial clearance, age above 21, and family consensus.
Complete absence of surgical risk and guaranteed clinical success.
questions.explanation: A valid consent requires patient comprehension, voluntary choice (free of pressure), full disclosure of information (informed), and decision-making capacity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What characterized the traditional and old concepts regarding breaking bad news?
options: Full immediate disclosure of all statistics to every relative.
Protective and authoritative attitudes where doctors acted as guardians of patient interest, sometimes withholding truth or deferring to relatives' wishes ("we do not want him to know").
Mandatory video-recording of all breaking bad news sessions.
Delegating all bad news delivery exclusively to hospital chaplains.
questions.explanation: Older paradigms relied on paternalistic, protective, and authoritative models where doctors shielded patients from distressing diagnoses.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What common pitfall was reported by patients and families who experienced suboptimal bad news encounters?
options: The physician was too compassionate and spent too much time talking.
The physician was too blunt, chose an inappropriate place/time, or gave the impression that there was zero hope.
The physician used overly simple language.
Too many written information leaflets were provided.
questions.explanation: Patients cited negative experiences when doctors were overly blunt, lacked sensitivity, created an inappropriate setting, or stripped away all hope.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What constitutes a common issue of concern or pitfall regarding informed consent in clinical practice?
options: Excessive patient comprehension and complete medical literacy.
Language barriers, cultural differences, time pressures, and inadequate documentation.
Over-abundance of time for patient reflection.
Complete transparency and zero information gaps.
questions.explanation: Pitfalls in consent include language barriers, cultural disparities, time constraints, incomplete disclosure, and treating patients with impaired decision-making.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes "Morals" from "Ethics" according to the lecture classifications?
options: Morals change rapidly with scientific development, whereas ethics are fixed.
Morals are internal values related to religion, culture, and personal beliefs, whereas ethics represent structured guidelines, professional standards, and character.
Ethical violations carry no legal consequences, whereas moral violations result in imprisonment.
Morals are determined by hospital committees, while ethics are private matters.
questions.explanation: Morals are internal, custom-based, and tied to personal/cultural beliefs, whereas ethics involve systematic guidelines, professional codes, and rules of conduct.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the "Invitation" (I) step in the SPIKES model involve?
options: Inviting hospital executives to witness the consultation.
Asking patients how much information they wish to know (e.g., "Would you like me to give you the full details or would you prefer I speak with a family member?").
Forcing every patient to review complete raw pathology slides.
Inviting legal counsel prior to discussing diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Invitation respects patient autonomy by asking how much detail they want to receive at that moment or if they prefer someone else to be briefed.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the "SPIKES" protocol stand for in the context of breaking bad news?
options: Symptoms, Prognosis, Investigation, Knowledge, Empathy, Support.
Setting up the interview, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, Strategy and summary.
Surgery, Patient inquiry, Key information, Evaluation, Solutions.
Screening, Pathology, Intervention, Communication, Execution, Safety.
questions.explanation: SPIKES is a structured 6-step model: Setting up, Perception, Invitation, Knowledge, Emotions, and Strategy/Summary.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the Deontology ethical theory primarily emphasize?
options: Universal utility and maximum societal pleasure.
Duties and obligations that must be fulfilled regardless of the consequences ("do the right thing because it is right").
questions.explanation: Deontology (derived from "deon", meaning duty in Greek) focuses on moral obligations and duties that must be upheld irrespective of outcomes .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the principle of Beneficence require of a physician?
options: To prioritize patient welfare above all and act with the intent of doing good.
To allow patients complete self-determination even if they lack capacity.
To remain completely neutral regarding treatment outcomes.
To distribute medical resources solely based on social status.
questions.explanation: Beneficence involves taking positive actions to help others, maintaining up-to-date knowledge, and ensuring patient welfare is the primary concern.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the principle of Justice (Equity) in medical ethics dictate?
options: Treating all patients identically regardless of clinical need.
Equitable distribution of health resources, benefits, and burdens irrespective of sex, religion, ethnicity, or social status.
Allocating advanced surgical care exclusively to high-paying individuals.
Prioritizing younger patients over older patients in every healthcare scenario.
questions.explanation: Justice ensures fair and equitable allocation of medical benefits and burdens without discrimination.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What does the principle of Veracity obligate physicians to uphold?
options: Absolute financial transparency with hospital administration.
Truth-telling and full, honest disclosure to patients.
Strict patient confidentiality under all criminal investigations.
Protection of public health data over individual rights.
questions.explanation: Veracity is the moral obligation of truth-telling and providing honest, full disclosures to patients.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is required when discussing alternative treatments during the informed consent process?
options: Explaining only the most expensive surgical alternative.
Explaining any alternative treatments along with their risks, benefits, and expected outcomes.
Discouraging patients from considering second opinions.
Focusing exclusively on the risks of refusing the doctor's preferred method.
questions.explanation: Informed consent mandates discussing alternative treatment options, their respective risks, benefits, and outcomes, alongside the consequences of refusing treatment.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the core focus of the Virtue ethical theory in medical practice?
options: Calculating the numerical ratio of benefits to harms.
Adhering strictly to universal rules regardless of outcomes.
Judging a person by their character and traits (such as honesty) rather than solely by isolated actions.
Distributing healthcare resources equitably across society
questions.explanation: Virtue theory focuses on the moral character of the individual (what makes a good person), emphasizing traits like honesty in all situations .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary distinction between medical ethics and the law?
options: The law is based on religion, whereas ethics is based strictly on hospital bylaws.
Ethics prescribes higher standards of behavior than does the law.
Ethics carries immediate prison sentences, whereas legal violations result in fines.
There is no overlap between legal obligations and ethical dutie
questions.explanation: Medical ethics prescribes higher standards of behavior than does the law, and physicians are occasionally required to adhere to ethical principles even when confronting flawed laws .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary goal of the final "Strategy and Summary" (S) step in SPIKES?
options: To summarize the discussion, establish a clear future care plan, schedule follow-up, explore patient ICE (ideas, concerns, expectations), and provide written info or support resources.
To dismiss the patient from outpatient care.
To prevent the patient from asking further questions.
questions.explanation: Strategy and summary ensure the patient leaves with a clear plan, understanding of future steps, available support services, and documentation in the medical record.
questions.topic: Breaking bad news: strategy and summary
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary legal and professional function of a signed written consent form?
options: To serve as an absolute shield against medical malpractice lawsuits.
To provide a documentary record showing that the patient was informed and agreed to the examination, test, treatment, or intervention.
To transfer all surgical risks onto the insurance company.
To replace verbal communication between doctor and patient.
questions.explanation: A written consent form serves as legal documentation confirming that the patient was properly informed and agreed to the specified procedure. Part 3: Breaking Bad News (Q35–Q50)
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary role of ethical codes such as the Declaration of Geneva and the Helsinki Declaration?
options: To replace national civil laws entirely.
To provide systematic ethical standards and guidelines for medical practice and clinical research.
To dictate hospital billing structures and insurance tariffs.
To restrict technological advancements in surgery.
questions.explanation: Declarations like Geneva and Helsinki serve as essential ethical benchmarks for medical professionalism and research integrity worldwide.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of assessing the patient's "Perception" (P) during SPIKES before delivering news?
options: To find out what the patient already knows, understand their expectations, and identify any denial or unrealistic beliefs.
To determine if they can pay for specialized oncology drugs.
To bypass the need for informed consent.
questions.explanation: Assessing perception ("What have other doctors told you?") helps the clinician tailor information to the patient's current understanding and mental state.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What legal recourse is available if a parent refuses life-saving treatment for their child?
options: The physician must discharge the child immediately.
The decision can be overruled by a court order to prevent death or severe permanent injury.
The nurse must perform the procedure without documentation.
Treatment cannot be rendered under any circumstance.
questions.explanation: When parental refusal threatens a child's life or risks permanent injury, the court can overrule the refusal to allow necessary medical care.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What must be communicated regarding the risks and complications during informed consent?
options: Only risks that have a 100% probability of occurring.
The specific risks and complications associated with the treatment or intervention, alongside expected benefits and outcomes.
Only minor bruising to avoid frightening the patient.
No risks should be mentioned to prevent patient anxiety.
questions.explanation: Patients must receive clear explanations regarding the necessity of treatment, anticipated outcomes, benefits, and potential risks or complications.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What role do relatives play when obtaining consent for an adult patient with full capacity?
options: Relatives hold absolute veto power over the patient's independent medical choices.
Relatives can be consulted for discussion if the patient allows, but a competent adult makes their own autonomous decisions.
Relatives must sign all consent forms on behalf of the patient.
Relatives are legally prohibited from entering the consultation room.
questions.explanation: Competent adults have self-determination; while they can discuss options with relatives or friends, the final decision rests with them.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What technique is recommended when sharing "Knowledge" (K) during the SPIKES interview?
options: Deliver all intricate pathological details rapidly in complex medical terminology.
Use a warning shot, start at the patient's comprehension level, use non-technical words (e.g., "spread" instead of "metastasis"), deliver information in small chunks, and pause frequently.
Send the diagnosis via an automated text message to avoid emotional confrontation.
Avoid mentioning any serious diagnosis until surgery is completed.
questions.explanation: Knowledge should be shared gently using warning shots ("I'm afraid it looks serious"), simple non-technical language, and digestible small chunks with pauses.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: When is a physician legally and ethically justified in breaking patient confidentiality?
options: When a colleague casually asks about an interesting case during lunch.
When required by law (e.g., reporting certain communicable diseases or child abuse) or to prevent imminent serious harm to others with patient consent where possible.
Whenever a family member demands details about an adult patient.
To publish case reports on social media without patient identifiers removed.
questions.explanation: Confidentiality must be maintained, but exceptions exist for public safety, statutory legal requirements, and prevention of severe harm.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which ethical principle is encapsulated by the maxim "First, do no harm"?
questions.explanation: Non-maleficence dictates that medical actions must not cause harm to the patient or others in society.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which ethical theory judges an act as morally permissible if it produces the greatest amount of good for the greatest number of persons affected?
questions.explanation: Consequentialism (utilitarianism) dictates that an action's morality is determined by whether its consequences yield the greatest good for the greatest number .
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which historical code established in 1948 arose directly in response to Nazi medical atrocities and set foundational standards for voluntary consent in human research?
questions.explanation: The Nuremberg Code (1948) established strict ethical requirements for human experimentation, emphasizing voluntary consent above all.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following comprises the four primary principles of Principlism in medical ethics?
questions.explanation: Principlism identifies four core pillars: respect for autonomy, non-maleficence, beneficence, and justice.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions can impair or disturb a person's mental capacity?
options: Acute intoxication caused by alcohol or drugs.
Mild routine fatigue after a normal night's sleep.
questions.explanation: Impairment of the mind due to mental health conditions, dementia, learning disabilities, brain damage, or drug/alcohol intoxication affects capacity.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements best summarizes the art of breaking bad news?
options: Bad news cannot be changed, but clinicians can learn specialized communication skills to deliver it compassionately, minimize distress, and provide realistic hope.
Breaking bad news is an innate personality trait that cannot be taught or learned through medical training.
Doctors should delegate bad news entirely to nurses to protect their own emotional well-being.
Minimizing the severity of the diagnosis is always the best ethical approach.
questions.explanation: While clinicians cannot alter the bad news itself, mastering structured communication models transforms the encounter, ensuring empathy, clarity, and sustained support.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which principle supports a competent adult patient's right to refuse life-saving medical treatment?
questions.explanation: Autonomy grants competent, well-informed adults the absolute right to accept or refuse any medical intervention or treatment.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Who is authorized to assess a patient's capacity to consent?
options: Only a certified psychiatrist or legal judge.
An appropriately trained and experienced healthcare professional who is either recommending or involved in carrying out the treatment or intervention.
Any family member designated by the household elder.
questions.explanation: Capacity should be assessed at the time consent is required by an appropriately trained clinician involved in the patient's care.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why do doctors and healthcare workers frequently experience anxiety or reluctance when breaking bad news?
options: Because they lack medical knowledge about the disease.
Fear of causing pain, distress, and suffering, fear of negative evaluation, uncertainty about patient response, and fear of blame.
Because hospital regulations forbid doctors from speaking directly to patients.
Because bad news is legally classified as a criminal offense.
questions.explanation: Clinicians often struggle with breaking bad news due to fears of causing distress, uncertainty, appearing incompetent, being blamed, or destroying hope.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is documentation of the bad news conversation critical?
options: It is solely used for medical legal defense against lawsuits.
It ensures continuity of care by making the information, patient reactions, and future plans known to the rest of the healthcare team and general practitioner.
It fulfills mandatory health insurance claim requirements.
It allows hospital archives to track mortality rates.
questions.explanation: Accurate documentation records what was communicated and the patient's reactions, facilitating seamless coordination among the medical team, GP, and support services.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Why is the study of diverse ethical theories vital for clinicians?
options: Because ethical dilemmas have a single mathematical solution.
Because ethical dilemmas have no single right answer, and clinicians must navigate complex choices respecting patient dignity and autonomy without relying on rigid, single-minded rules.
To eliminate the need for hospital ethics committees.
To ensure doctors never face malpractice litigation.
questions.explanation: Ethics is not a rigid prescription; recognizing multiple ethical frameworks helps clinicians rationally resolve complex moral dilemmas. Part 2: Consent & Capacity (Q18–Q34)
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 7-day post-hemorrhoidectomy patient presents with brisk arterial bleeding from the wound site. How is this hemorrhage classified?
questions.explanation: Bleeding occurring a week after surgery (7 to 14 days) is classified as secondary hemorrhage, typically due to infection and vessel erosion.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A trauma patient continues to bleed intraoperatively and develops the lethal triad of hypothermia (34°C), acidosis (pH 7.1), and coagulopathy (INR 2.2). What is the best immediate surgical strategy?
options: Perform damage control surgery focused on rapid bleeding control and physiological stabilization.
Close the abdomen immediately and transfer to an unmonitored ward.
questions.explanation: Damage control surgery prioritizes halting hemorrhage, packing, and temporary closure to correct the lethal triad rather than prolonged definitive surgery.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: According to ATLS guidelines, what percentage of blood volume loss characterizes Class I hemorrhagic shock?
questions.explanation: Class I hemorrhage involves < 15% blood loss (< 750 mL) and is typically asymptomatic with normal vital signs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: During which stage of shock does a patient exhibit normal blood pressure, tachycardia, and selective redistribution of blood flow to vital organs (brain, heart, adrenals)?
questions.explanation: In compensated shock, autonomic homeostatic mechanisms maintain blood pressure despite reduced perfusion by shunting blood to vital organs.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: How is surgical bleeding classified if it occurs within 24 hours following a surgical procedure due to slipped ligatures or dislodged clots?
questions.explanation: Reactionary hemorrhage occurs within 24 hours post-op due to factors like blood pressure restoration or slipped vessel ligatures.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In Class IV hemorrhagic shock (> 40% blood volume loss), what is the expected hourly urine output?
questions.explanation: In Class IV shock, severe renal vasoconstriction causes profound oliguria or negligible urine output (5–15 mL/hour).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: In the management of septic shock (a subset of distributive shock), what is the first-line vasopressor of choice when fluid resuscitation fails to restore adequate mean arterial pressure (MAP)?
questions.explanation: Norepinephrine is the primary vasopressor recommended in septic shock to restore vascular tone and target a MAP > 65 mm Hg.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What classic electrocardiographic (ECG) changes appear earliest during moderate to severe hyperkalemia (serum level 5.5–6.5 mEq/L)?
options: Prominent U waves and depressed ST segments
Tall, peaked T waves and wide QRS complexes
Prolonged QT intervals with flat T waves
questions.explanation: Hyperkalemia characteristically presents with tall, peaked T waves, progressing to prolonged PR intervals, widened QRS, loss of P waves, and sinusoidal waves.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What distinguishes distributive shock from hypovolemic and cardiogenic shock regarding peripheral vascular tone?
options: Severe peripheral vasoconstriction with cold extremities.
Marked peripheral vasodilation resulting in low SVR and initially warm extremities.
Complete absence of autonomic nervous regulation.
questions.explanation: Distributive shock (septic, anaphylactic, neurogenic) is characterized by severe peripheral vasodilation and low systemic vascular resistance.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What effect does extracellular fluid (ECF) acidosis have on serum potassium balance?
options: Causes hypokalemia via intracellular potassium trapping.
Causes hyperkalemia as hydrogen ions move into cells in exchange for potassium moving out.
Has no measurable impact on transmembrane potassium flux.
questions.explanation: In ECF acidosis, excess extracellular hydrogen ions shift into cells in exchange for potassium, leading to hyperkalemia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What hemodynamic profile (PCWP/JVP, Cardiac Output, Systemic Vascular Resistance) is characteristic of hypovolemic shock?
options: Decreased PCWP, Decreased CO, Increased SVR
Increased PCWP, Decreased CO, Increased SVR
Decreased PCWP, Increased CO, Decreased SVR
Increased PCWP, Increased CO, Decreased SVR
questions.explanation: In hypovolemic shock, intravascular volume loss leads to low filling pressures (low PCWP/JVP) and low cardiac output (CO), with compensatory high systemic vascular resistance (SVR).
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is a hallmark finding in neurogenic shock compared to most other forms of shock?
options: Bradycardia (or relative bradycardia) combined with hypotension due to loss of sympathetic tone
questions.explanation: Neurogenic shock (from spinal cord injury or high sympathetic block) disrupts sympathetic pathways, resulting in hypotension accompanied by bradycardia.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is defined as hypernatremia in terms of seru9m sodium concentration?
questions.explanation: Hypernatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration exceeding 145 mEq/L, reflecting serum hyperosmolality.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the clinical significance of finding a flat inferior vena cava (IVC ≤ 2.1 cm with > 50% collapse) on bedside ultrasound in a shocked patient?
options: Severe fluid overload and right heart failure.
Low central venous pressure consistent with hypovolemia or distributive shock.
questions.explanation: A collapsible, small IVC reflects low volume status or low central venous pressure, pointing toward hypovolemic or distributive states.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the fundamental pathophysiological definition of shock?
options: A primary neurological reflex causing transient syncope.
A clinical state of circulatory collapse and failure characterized by reduced tissue perfusion leading to tissue hypoxia and acidosis.
Isolated systolic hypertension refractory to fluid administration.
Primary renal failure resulting in uremic encephalopathy.
questions.explanation: Shock represents systemic circulatory failure resulting in inadequate tissue perfusion, cellular hypoxia, and metabolic acidosis.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the initial, immediate fluid resuscitation strategy in managing a surgical patient presenting with acute hemorrhagic or hypovolemic shock?
options: Immediate administration of 5% Dextrose in water.
Insertion of large-bore IV cannulae and infusion of isotonic crystalloids (normal saline or lactated Ringer's) / blood products.
questions.explanation: Initial resuscitation requires secure access with large-bore cannulae and rapid replacement using crystalloids or blood products according to protocols.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the most common electrolyte disorder encountered among hospitalized patients, with a prevalence of 20%–30%?
questions.explanation: Hyponatremia (serum sodium < 135 mEq/L) is the most common electrolyte disturbance in hospital settings, particularly among the elderly.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the most common underlying cause of secondary hemorrhage, typically occurring 7 to 14 days post-operatively?
questions.explanation: Secondary hemorrhage is delayed (days to weeks) and is typically caused by localized infection, inflammation, and subsequent vessel erosion or sloughing.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the normal physiological range for plasma osmolality in a healthy adult?
questions.explanation: Normal plasma osmolality is tightly regulated around 280–295 mosmol/kg.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the physiological consequence of infusing an isotonic sodium chloride solution into the intravascular space?
options: Expands both ECF and ICF equally via active osmosis.
Increases extracellular fluid (ECF) volume without shifting fluid across cellular membranes.
Decreases intravascular volume while expanding intracellular volume.
questions.explanation: Isotonic NaCl stays largely within the extracellular compartment, increasing ECF volume. Part 2: Hemorrhage in Surgery
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary cause of shock in a patient who develops sudden hypotension, distended neck veins (high JVP), tracheal deviation, and absent unilateral breath sounds after central line placement?
options: Obstructive shock due to tension pneumothorax
questions.explanation: Tension pneumothorax obstructs venous return, causing obstructive shock with elevated JVP and absent breath sounds.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary hormonal regulator responsible for controlling plasma sodium concentration and free water balance?
questions.explanation: ADH regulates free water reabsorption in the renal collecting ducts, making it the primary regulator for plasma sodium concentration.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the primary mechanism responsible for decreased serum sodium levels in water excess / water intoxication states frequently seen postoperatively in elderly patients?
options: Administration of hypotonic fluids (like 5% dextrose) combined with non-osmotic ADH release.
Primary renal tubular hyper-reabsorption of bicarbonate.
questions.explanation: Water excess in postoperative elderly patients often results from infusing 5% dextrose solutions coupled with surgical stress-induced ADH release.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: What is the recommended daily dietary sodium intake limit referenced in fluid and electrolyte management?

questions.stem: What pulse pressure characteristic is typically observed in Class II and Class III hemorrhagic shock?

questions.stem: Which conditions are classic examples of obstructive (restrictive) shock?

Spinal cord transection and neurogenic vasodilation

questions.stem: Which ion is the principal intracellular cation?

questions.stem: Which of the following clinical parameters represents the earliest objective sign of acute hypovolemic shock in a surgical patient?
questions.explanation: Tachycardia is an early compensatory autonomic response to maintain cardiac output before overt systolic hypotension manifests.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions can cause distributive shock?
questions.explanation: Sepsis, anaphylaxis, and neurogenic injury are primary etiologies of distributive shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following conditions does NOT cause distributive shock?
options: Severe emotional vasovagal syncopal episode / neurogenic reflex

questions.stem: Which of the following electrolyte imbalances is characteristically associated with ECG showing a prominent U wave, depressed ST segment, and diphasic T wave?
questions.explanation: Hypokalemia classically alters cardiac repolarization, producing ST depression, flattened or diphasic T waves, and prominent U waves.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings is common across almost all types of shock?
questions.explanation: Inadequate tissue perfusion leads to anaerobic metabolism and lactic acid accumulation, resulting in metabolic acidosis across most forms of shock.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: Which of the following fluid spaces is considered part of transcellular fluid?
questions.explanation: Transcellular fluid (making up about 1% of TBW) includes fluids such as CSF, synovial fluid, and gastrointestinal secretions.

questions.stem: Which of the following parameters is monitored hourly as a sensitive indicator of visceral and renal perfusion during shock resuscitation?

questions.stem: Which physiological parameter change is expected in cardiogenic shock?
options: Increased PCWP / JVP (due to pump failure)

questions.stem: Within what timeframe from injury or bleeding onset is Tranexamic acid (TXA) most effective?
questions.explanation: Clinical evidence and surgical guidelines emphasize that TXA must be given within 3 hours of bleeding onset for optimal mortality benefit.

questions.stem: A 39-year-old, 80-kg trauma patient is intubated and sedated in the ICU. Based on standard surgical ICU calculations (25–30 kcal/kg/day), what is their approximate daily calorie goal?
questions.explanation: Severely ill patients require roughly 25–30 kcal/kg/day; for an 80-kg patient, this yields a target range around 2,000–2,400 kcal/day (fitting option C).

questions.stem: How can clinicians best minimize or manipulate the surgical metabolic response before and during an operation?
options: Delaying pain management until postoperative day 3
Utilizing minimally invasive surgery, careful tissue handling, controlling pain, and correcting shock
Keeping the operating room at freezing temperatures

questions.stem: How long does the ebb phase of the metabolic response to injury typically last?
questions.explanation: The ebb phase is the period of shock immediately following the insult, lasting roughly 24–48 hours, and is characterized by a decrease in metabolic rate and oxygen consumption.

questions.stem: In severe cases of trauma complicated by impaired tissue perfusion and shock, what acid-base disturbance characteristically develops?
options: Metabolic acidosis (due to lactic acid accumulation)
questions.explanation: While mild sodium retention can cause metabolic alkalosis, severe impaired tissue perfusion and anaerobic metabolism lead to lactic acidosis.

questions.stem: In surgical patients, what is the clinical impact of early enteral feeding compared to delayed feeding?
options: Increased rate of wound infections and anastomotic leaks
Reduced mortality, fewer complications, and shorter hospital stays

questions.stem: In the daily laboratory monitoring of a patient on TPN, which lab test must be checked daily?

questions.stem: Peripheral insulin resistance following major trauma directly contributes to which metabolic abnormality?

questions.stem: Preoperative malnutrition is strongly associated with which adverse clinical outcomes?

Higher rates of surgical site infection, impaired wound healing, and pressure ulcers

questions.stem: The metabolic response after major surgery is classically associated with which of the following?

questions.stem: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) is strictly indicated in which of the following clinical scenarios?

Post-operative day 1 after a routine elective colonic resection with normal recovery
Severe acute pancreatitis with paralytic ileus or high-output enterocutaneous fistulas
Patient with mild self-limiting dysphagia for 24 hours

questions.stem: What causes the dilutional hyponatremia frequently observed following severe trauma or surgery?
options: Impaired water and sodium excretion driven by Arginine Vasopressin (ADH) and aldosterone
Rapid loss of potassium via the skin

questions.stem: What does the ERAS (Enhanced Recovery After Surgery) protocol emphasize regarding post-operative nutrition?
options: Keeping patients fasting for 5 days post-op to rest the bowel
Early oral feeding as soon as possible and minimizing unnecessary fasting periods
Relying exclusively on total parenteral nutrition for all abdominal cases
Restricting all fluids until bowel sounds return

questions.stem: What is a critical mechanical complication associated with nasogastric or feeding tube placement?

questions.stem: What is a defining hallmark of the catabolic flow phase?

questions.topic: Metabolic response to trauma: catabolic flow phase

questions.stem: What is a major proven advantage of enteral nutrition over parenteral nutrition?
options: It requires multiple complex daily blood tests.
It maintains gut mucosal integrity and prevents mucosal thinning.
It carries a higher risk of systemic catheter sepsis.
It requires a central venous line insertion.

questions.stem: What is the effect of Arginine Vasopressin (AVP / ADH) and Aldosterone release during the immediate post-injury period?

Direct vasodilation of peripheral capillary beds
Stimulation of insulin secretion from the pancreas

options: It is significantly cheaper and easier to administer without any monitoring.
It maintains the gastrointestinal mucosal defense barrier and prevents mucosal atrophy.

It stops all forms of muscle proteolysis instantly.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a 2‑cm, firm, mobile mass in the left upper quadrant. Imaging shows a well‑defined encapsulated lesion arising from the left adrenal gland. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
questions.explanation: The lesion is small, well‑defined, and asymptomatic, suggesting a benign adenoma. The preferred treatment is minimally invasive removal if surgery is indicated. Laparoscopic adrenalectomy (option D) offers equivalent oncologic outcomes with less morbidity compared to open surgery. Fine‑needle aspiration (option B) is contraindicated for adrenal masses due to risk of tumor seeding and does not provide therapeutic benefit. Observation (option C) is reasonable only if the mass is definitively benign and the patient is low risk; however, surgical removal is often recommended for masses >4 cm or symptomatic. Immediate open surgery (option A) is unnecessarily invasive.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 45‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of intermittent right upper quadrant pain, nausea and a palpable mass in the right hypochondrium. Imaging shows a 6‑cm heterogeneous lesion arising from the liver with a central scar and a hypervascular rim. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step in management?
options: A. 3‑month interval imaging to assess growth
C. Surgical resection with segmental hepatectomy
questions.explanation: The imaging characteristics (heterogeneous lesion with central scar and hypervascular rim) are classic for a hepatocellular carcinoma in a non‑cirrhotic liver. The lesion is >5 cm and symptomatic, so the standard of care is surgical resection with a segmental hepatectomy. Observation (A) would miss the opportunity for curative surgery. Percutaneous biopsy (B) is contraindicated in suspected HCC because it can seed tumour cells and does not alter management. Transarterial chemoembolization (D) is reserved for unresectable or palliative disease, not for a resectable tumour.
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

questions.stem: A 68‑year‑old man presents with a 3‑month history of progressive dysphagia to solids, weight loss, and a palpable left supraclavicular lymph node. Endoscopy shows a circumferential ulcerating lesion at the gastro‑oesophageal junction. Biopsy confirms poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. In the absence of distant metastasis, which of the following operative strategies provides the best chance of long‑term survival while preserving adequate postoperative quality of life?
options: A. 180° total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy
B. 180° total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and prophylactic splenectomy
C. 180° total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and regional lymph node sampling
D. 180° total gastrectomy with D2 lymphadenectomy and a simultaneous splenectomy for tumour extension
questions.explanation: The tumour is located at the gastro‑oesophageal junction and is poorly differentiated, indicating aggressive biology. The optimal surgical approach is a 180° total gastrectomy with a D2 lymphadenectomy, which provides adequate oncologic clearance for junctional tumours. Splenectomy is not routinely indicated unless the tumour directly invades the splenic hilum; routine prophylactic splenectomy increases morbidity without survival benefit. Therefore option A is the best choice. Option B adds unnecessary splenectomy, option C offers insufficient nodal clearance, and option D unnecessarily adds splenectomy for tumour extension that is not present.
questions.source: Principles of oncologic resection for gastro‑oesophageal junction tumours
questions.topic: Principles of oncologic resection for gastro‑oesophageal junction tumours
questions.approvalNote: Approved by the supervising physician per project instruction on 2026-11-15.

Routine blood count followed by immediate surgery without biopsy
Plain abdominal radiography and trial of antibiotics

The percentage of people who are alive five years after their initial cancer diagnosis.

To accelerate the catabolic flow phase of metabolism.

questions.stem: Blood Glucose Management In the intensive care management of a patient recovering from septic shock, what is the target blood glucose range recommended by consensus guidelines?

questions.stem: Definitions (Sepsis-3 Criteria) According to the Sepsis-3 consensus definitions, septic shock is clinically identified by sepsis plus which two mandatory criteria?
options: Persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors to maintain \text{MAP} \ge 65\text{ mmHg} AND a serum lactate > 2\text{ mmol/L} despite adequate fluid resuscitation
White blood cell count > 12,000/\text{mm}^3 AND heart rate > 100\text{ bpm}
Positive blood cultures AND a core temperature < 35^\circ\text{C}
Elevated serum creatinine > 2.0\text{ mg/dL} AND mild transaminitis
questions.explanation: The Sepsis-3 definition specifically separates septic shock as a subset of sepsis where underlying circulatory, cellular, and metabolic abnormalities are profound enough to substantially increase mortality, operationalized by persistent hypotension requiring vasopressors and hyperlactatemia despite fluid resuscitation.

questions.stem: Enteral vs. Parenteral Nutrition Regarding nutritional support during the acute resuscitation phase of septic shock, which approach is currently recommended once the patient is hemodynamically stable?

Complete fasting (nil per os) until all vasopressors are entirely discontinued for 5 days
Early enteral nutrition (trophic feeds) initiated within 24 to 48 hours
